achondroplasia.name: Achondroplasia
achondroplasia.scope: FGFR3 gene mutation, impaired endochondral ossification, rhizomelic dwarfism, macrocephaly, frontal bossing, spinal stenosis risk, autosomal dominant with advanced paternal age
achondroplasia.core: Disproportionately short limbs with relatively preserved trunk length, large head, and characteristic facial shape; early neurologic assessment prevents fatal compression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Autosomal dominant**, high penetrance; most cases de novo; advanced paternal age increases new mutations

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Rhizomelic shortening**, macrocephaly, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, trident hands; normal intelligence
Lumbar lordosis, bowed legs, infant hypotonia; motor milestones may be delayed
Apnea, hyperreflexia, clonus, weakness → craniocervical compression; progressive leg symptoms → lumbar canal narrowing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ **FGFR3 gain-of-function** inhibits growth-plate chondrocytes → impaired endochondral ossification
Intramembranous bone formation relatively preserved; skull base narrowing explains early neurologic danger

rows.label: Dx
items: Proportions + skeletal radiographs; short long bones, caudally narrowing interpedicular distances, square pelvis
**FGFR3 testing** confirms uncertain cases and supports reproductive counseling
★ Infancy: neurologic examination, polysomnography, **craniocervical MRI** to evaluate foramen magnum compression
Track head circumference on achondroplasia-specific curves; rapid acceleration → hydrocephalus evaluation

rows.label: Tx

Obstructive sleep apnea → adenotonsillectomy/CPAP; recurrent effusions → tympanostomy tubes
Specialist-selected **vosoritide**, CNP analog, improves growth with open growth plates; monitor hypotension
Growth hormone provides limited benefit; orthopedic care and functional adaptations support mobility

rows.label: Complications
items: Sudden infant death from cervicomedullary compression; hydrocephalus, hearing impairment, obesity, degenerative joint disease
Adult lumbar stenosis → neurogenic claudication or cauda equina syndrome

rows.label: Prevention
items: Support infant neck; avoid unsupported sitting and contact sports; regular hearing and sleep assessment
Genetic counseling; discuss prenatal testing and recurrence from possible germline mosaicism

rows.label: Mimics

Osteogenesis imperfecta: fragility fractures, blue sclerae; endocrine short stature: proportionate body segments

acid-base-disorders.name: Acid-base disorders
acid-base-disorders.scope: Metabolic acidosis (anion gap, non-anion gap), metabolic alkalosis (saline-responsive vs saline-resistant), respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, Winter formula, mixed disorders
acid-base-disorders.core: Identify the primary pH disturbance, test expected compensation, then investigate the anion gap or urine chloride to locate the cause.

rows.label: Definition
items: Acidemia: pH <7.35; alkalemia: >7.45; normal pH can hide opposing primary disorders
Metabolic: primary HCO3 change; respiratory: primary PaCO2 change

rows.label: Formula
items: ★ **AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3)**; usual normal ≈8–12, laboratory dependent
Hypoalbuminemia correction: add 2.5 to AG per 1 g/dL albumin below 4
★ **Winter: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ±2**

rows.label: Interpret
items: HCO3 12 → expected PaCO2 26 ±2; measured 40 → additional respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis: expected PaCO2 ≈40 + 0.7 × (HCO3 − 24), ±5
Respiratory HCO3 change per 10 PaCO2: acidosis +1 acute/+4 chronic; alkalosis −2 acute/−4 chronic

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Alkalosis: **urine Cl <20 mmol/L** → saline-responsive; ≥20 → diuretics/mineralocorticoids
ΔAG exceeds HCO3 fall → additional alkalosis; smaller ΔAG → additional non-gap acidosis

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Compensation never overshoots; values outside expected range imply **mixed disorder**
Salicylates often cause respiratory alkalosis plus high-gap acidosis; near-normal pH is deceptive
Diarrhea/RTA: non-gap acidosis; distal RTA: urine pH >5.5, hypokalemia; renal failure: either gap pattern

acid-base-disorders.evidence: Established physiologic formulas; no guideline involved.

alpha-1-antitrypsin-deficiency.scope: SERPINA1 gene mutation (PiZZ phenotype), panacinar basilar emphysema in young nonsmokers, liver cirrhosis/hepatoma, PAS-positive diastase-resistant globules, serum AAT level and phenotype

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autosomal codominant **SERPINA1** variants; PiZZ phenotype causes severe deficiency

rows.label: Clues

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Serum AAT level** → phenotype or genotype confirmation; acute inflammation can falsely elevate levels

amenorrhea.name: Amenorrhea
amenorrhea.scope: Primary amenorrhea (Turner syndrome, Mullerian agenesis, AIS), secondary amenorrhea (pregnancy, functional hypothalamic, hyperprolactinemia, thyroid, premature ovarian insufficiency, Asherman), diagnostic algorithm
amenorrhea.core: Absent menses requires pregnancy exclusion, then assessment of anatomy, estrogen status, thyroid function, prolactin, and the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Weight loss, intense exercise, psychosocial stress; pituitary disease, dopamine-blocking drugs, thyroid dysfunction

rows.label: Clues
items: Primary: no menarche by 15; absent breast development by 13 also warrants evaluation
Secondary: ≥3 months absent previously regular cycles, or ≥6 months previously irregular

Galactorrhea, hypothyroid signs → TSH first (TRH raises prolactin); unexplained prolactin → pituitary MRI

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Amenorrhea results from axis suppression, ovarian failure, chronic anovulation, or absent/obstructed outflow

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **hCG first**, even if unlikely or premenarchal (ovulation precedes menarche); ultrasound assesses uterus, ovaries
★ TSH, prolactin, **FSH/estradiol**; low estradiol: high FSH → ovarian failure; low/normal FSH → hypothalamic/pituitary
**Progestin challenge**: bleed → anovulation (estrogen, outflow intact); no bleed → low estrogen/outflow defect, check FSH
POI before 40: ≥4 months irregular/absent cycles with FSH >25 IU/L; repeat if uncertain
Post-instrumentation amenorrhea with otherwise normal endocrine testing → saline sonography/hysteroscopy for adhesions

rows.label: Tx

★ POI → **estrogen replacement plus progestogen if uterus present**, usually until natural menopause age
Chronic anovulation → endometrial protection with cyclic progestogen or combined contraception; treat underlying cause
Hematocolpos → **transvaginal incision, drainage**; imperforate hymen → **cruciate hymenotomy**; ultrasound if anatomy unclear

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoestrogenism → infertility, low bone density; prolonged unopposed estrogen → endometrial hyperplasia
Absent uterus differs from absent ovaries: fertility options depend on anatomy and gonadal function

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate nutrition, avoid overtraining/uterine injury; intermittent ovulation still requires contraception

rows.label: Mimics

PCOS: hyperandrogenism with chronic anovulation, estrogen generally preserved

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.scope: Diagnosis, stepwise therapy, acute exacerbation, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction
asthma.core: Variable episodes of wheeze, cough, dyspnea, and chest tightness from reversible expiratory airflow limitation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: **Family history of asthma/atopy**: strongest childhood risk; allergens, viral infections, smoke, occupational sensitizers
Exercise/cold air, aspirin-sensitive disease, nonselective beta-blockers; assess workplace symptom pattern

rows.label: Clues
items: Nocturnal/early-morning symptoms; normal examination between attacks
★ **Silent chest, exhaustion, altered mentation, rising PaCO2** → impending respiratory failure
Acute attack: low peak flow, accessory-muscle use, difficulty speaking
Cough-variant: isolated chronic cough, worse with cold/exercise; normal examination and radiograph

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Allergen cross-links IgE on **mast cells** → histamine, leukotrienes → bronchoconstriction
Airway inflammation, smooth-muscle constriction, mucus → variable obstruction and hyperresponsiveness
Persistent uncontrolled inflammation → remodeling with incompletely reversible airflow limitation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Spirometry**: obstruction with bronchodilator FEV1 increase >12% and >200 mL in adults
Normal spirometry with suspicion → repeat during symptoms or methacholine challenge
Exercise challenge: postexercise FEV1 fall >10%; assess baseline control before isolated exercise diagnosis
PFT pattern: ↓FEV1, normal/↓FVC, normal/↑TLC from air trapping

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Exacerbation → **repeated inhaled albuterol + ipratropium**, oxygen, early systemic glucocorticoids
Severe poor response → IV magnesium; deterioration → intubation; avoid sedatives and routine antibiotics
Exercise symptoms → preexercise albuterol or prescribed ICS-formoterol; persistent symptoms → improve controller
Check technique/adherence before stepping up; uncontrolled despite high-dose ICS-LABA → phenotype-directed biologic referral
Discharge: **PEF ≥70–80% predicted** (less wheeze is unreliable) + 5–7 day **oral prednisone** prevents relapse

rows.label: Complications
items: Status asthmaticus, pneumothorax, respiratory arrest
ICS → thrush/dysphonia; systemic steroids → osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Written action plan, trigger reduction, smoking cessation, spacer; rinse mouth after ICS
★ GINA: **no SABA-only treatment**, no LABA monotherapy; ICS with every reliever use
Older exam questions (NAEPP) may expect: symptoms ≤2 days/week, awakenings ≤2/month → **SABA alone**; more → daily ICS

COPD: persistent obstruction, smoking history
HF: edema, elevated JVP, cardiac findings
Deconditioning: obese/sedentary, exertional dyspnea; normal PFTs, no bronchodilator response

Traction/compression can injure nerves; spontaneous delivery does not exclude neonatal trauma

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Increasing head circumference, pallor, tachycardia, poor perfusion** → concealed scalp hemorrhage until proven otherwise
Asymmetric Moro response → fracture or brachial plexus injury; inspect spontaneous movement and grasp
Clavicular crepitus/tenderness or later callus; pain-limited movement can mimic neurologic weakness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Scalp compartments differ in capacity and suture boundaries; broad potential spaces permit major blood loss
Peripheral compression causes neurapraxia; traction may produce more severe plexus disruption

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical scalp examination plus **serial head circumference and hematocrit** when bleeding suspected
Trend vitals/perfusion; CBC, coagulation studies, crossmatch for expanding swelling
Suspected fracture → clavicle radiograph if uncertain; assess joints and distinguish pain from paralysis
Facial injury: asymmetric cry and incomplete eyelid closure; examine forehead to localize peripheral palsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Shock/expanding subgaleal collection → **NICU, IV resuscitation and blood products** immediately
★ Cephalohematoma: observe bilirubin/hematocrit; **never aspirate routinely** because infection risk
Clavicular fracture → gentle handling, analgesia, brief immobilization; usually heals rapidly
Plexus injury → gentle range-of-motion/physical treatment, early follow-up; persistent deficits → specialist
Facial palsy → lubricate/protect incompletely closing eye; most compression injuries recover over weeks

rows.label: Complications
items: Blood breakdown → jaundice; massive hemorrhage → anemia, DIC, shock
Severe plexus injury → contractures and persistent weakness; corneal injury with incomplete closure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Careful instrument selection/traction, shoulder-dystocia maneuvers and team training; postinstrument delivery surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Congenital muscular torticollis: sternocleidomastoid tightness rather than limb weakness
Central neurologic injury: seizures, altered alertness, broader motor abnormalities

table.title: Localization
rows: Subcutaneous edema; crosses sutures; resolves days
Subperiosteal blood; does not cross sutures; resolves weeks
Diffuse boggy expanding swelling; crosses sutures
Waiter's tip; absent Moro, preserved grasp
Weak hand/grasp; possible ipsilateral Horner syndrome

birth-trauma.evidence: Not checked online; established neonatal trauma recognition and stabilization teaching.

bite-wounds.name: Bite wounds
bite-wounds.scope: Cat bites (Pasteurella multocida), dog bites, human bites (Eikenella corrodens), wound irrigation, closure vs secondary intention, amoxicillin-clavulanate, rabies and tetanus prophylaxis
bite-wounds.core: Animal or human bites combine tissue damage with polymicrobial inoculation; hand injuries and deep punctures carry disproportionate infection risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Cat punctures, delayed presentation, diabetes, immunosuppression, asplenia, wounds near joints
Clenched-fist injury over MCP joint → occult human bite with possible tendon penetration

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid pain, erythema, swelling, drainage; infection may appear within hours after a cat bite
★ Pain with passive movement, restricted motion, systemic toxicity → **deep-space infection**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mixed aerobes/anaerobes introduced below skin; narrow punctures trap organisms
Crush injury and devitalized tissue impair clearance; tendon sheaths permit proximal spread

rows.label: Dx
items: Neurovascular/tendon examination; assess joint penetration and retained foreign material
Radiograph for hand fight bite, suspected tooth fragment, bone injury, or osteomyelitis
Culture infected drainage; no routine culture of an uninfected fresh wound

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Copious irrigation + debridement**; hand elevation, assess need for surgical exploration
★ Human/cat/hand bite prophylaxis or infection → **amoxicillin-clavulanate**; severe → IV ampicillin-sulbactam
Prophylaxis usually 3–5 days; established infection needs longer, guided by depth and response
★ Hand or human bites, punctures, infected wounds → **leave open**; clean facial lacerations → primary closure
Rabies-risk exposure: unvaccinated → wound HRIG + vaccine days 0, 3, 7, 14; immunocompromised add 28

rows.label: Complications
items: Tenosynovitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, bacteremia; asplenia → fulminant Capnocytophaga sepsis
Rabies almost universally fatal after symptoms begin

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Dirty wound: **tetanus booster if ≥5 years**; unknown/incomplete series → vaccine + TIG
Prior rabies vaccination → vaccine days 0, 3; no HRIG; public health assesses animal risk
Healthy dog/cat/ferret available → 10-day observation coordinated with public health; animal-handling education

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonbite cellulitis: no inoculation history or puncture
Crystal arthritis: joint inflammation with crystals, but aspiration still needed if infection possible

table.title: Characteristic pathogens
rows: Eikenella corrodens; mixed oral/skin flora, anaerobes

bronchiolitis.name: Bronchiolitis
bronchiolitis.scope: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), infant wheezing, respiratory distress, hypoxemia, supplemental oxygen, nasal suctioning, palivizumab prophylaxis indications
bronchiolitis.core: Infant with a viral prodrome followed by a first episode of diffuse wheezing or crackles: supportive care is the main treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age <2 years, winter exposure, daycare; RSV commonest cause
Severe disease: age <12 weeks, prematurity, chronic lung disease, significant congenital heart disease, immunodeficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachypnea, retractions, nasal flaring, reduced intake; examination may fluctuate after suctioning
★ Apnea, exhaustion, cyanosis, dehydration → admission and escalation
Very young infants may present with apnea without prominent lower-airway findings

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Viral injury → small-airway edema, mucus plugging, air trapping, patchy atelectasis
Ventilation–perfusion mismatch causes hypoxemia; tiny infant airways increase obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; no routine chest radiograph, viral testing, CBC, or blood cultures
Assess work of breathing, hydration, and oxygenation; investigate focal findings or atypical course
Radiographic atelectasis can mimic pneumonia and drive unnecessary antibiotics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Gentle **nasal suctioning** + small frequent feeds; NG/IV fluids if intake inadequate
★ Persistent SpO2 <90% → oxygen; worsening distress → high-flow support, CPAP/intubation if failing
No routine albuterol, epinephrine, corticosteroids, antibiotics, or chest physiotherapy
Antibiotics only for documented/suspected bacterial coinfection; avoid deep repetitive suctioning

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, apnea, dehydration; later recurrent wheezing association
Cough may persist for weeks despite improving respiratory effort

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Hand hygiene, smoke avoidance; maternal RSV vaccine or infant antibody protection
Age <8 months: nirsevimab/clesrovimab if maternal vaccination absent/unknown or birth <14 days afterward
Age 8–19 months, second season: nirsevimab for selected high-risk children, including severe immunocompromise
Palivizumab: historical board option; US availability ended 2025; current long-acting antibodies replace it

rows.label: Mimics
items: Asthma: recurrent episodes, older child, atopic history
Foreign body: abrupt onset, unilateral wheeze
Bacterial pneumonia: focal consolidation, toxic appearance

caustic-ingestion.name: Caustic ingestion
caustic-ingestion.scope: Acid and alkali ingestion, airway assessment, contraindications to emesis or neutralization, early esophagogastroduodenoscopy within 24 hours, stricture complications
caustic-ingestion.core: Corrosive ingestion can burn the airway and gastrointestinal tract; a normal mouth examination does not exclude deep injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young children: accidental household cleaner exposure; adults: intentional large-volume ingestion
Drain/oven cleaners (NaOH), industrial acids; bleach usually mild; concentration, contact time determine severity

rows.label: Clues
items: Oral burns/ulcers, drooling, odynophagia, dysphagia, vomiting, hematemesis, chest or abdominal pain
★ **Stridor, hoarseness, respiratory distress** → threatened airway
Severe tenderness, rigidity, fever, shock → transmural necrosis or perforation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alkali: liquefactive necrosis, deep esophageal penetration; acid: coagulative necrosis, often gastric injury
Both agents can injure the entire upper gastrointestinal tract; eschar provides incomplete protection

rows.label: Dx
items: Identify substance, concentration, amount, time; poison control consultation
★ Stable symptomatic/significant exposure → **EGD within 24 hours** for injury grading
Suspected perforation/necrosis → contrast CT chest/abdomen and surgery consultation; avoid diagnostic endoscopy if perforated
CBC, electrolytes, renal function, lactate, blood gas; normal labs cannot exclude injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Airway first**; early controlled intubation with direct visualization when swelling progresses
NPO, IV crystalloid, analgesia; surgical treatment for perforation or full-thickness necrosis
★ **No emesis, neutralization, gastric lavage, or activated charcoal**; additional burns or heat generation
Avoid blind NG placement; no routine corticosteroids or prophylactic antibiotics

rows.label: Complications
items: Mediastinitis, peritonitis, hemorrhage, fistula; delayed esophageal stricture or gastric outlet obstruction
Long-term esophageal squamous cell carcinoma risk; strictures may require repeated dilation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Locked storage in original labeled containers; never transfer chemicals into beverage bottles
Intentional ingestion → psychiatric assessment after stabilization; swallowing/nutrition follow-up after severe injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Esophageal foreign body: discrete obstruction on history or imaging
Pill esophagitis: medication exposure, focal ulceration without extensive chemical burns

caustic-ingestion.evidence: Not checked online; established toxicology teaching.

child-abuse-and-neglect.name: Child abuse and neglect
child-abuse-and-neglect.scope: Physical abuse (burn patterns, fractures of different ages, metaphyseal corner fractures), abusive head trauma (shaken baby, subdural hematoma, retinal hemorrhages), neglect, mandatory reporting
child-abuse-and-neglect.core: Reasonable suspicion of child maltreatment requires protective reporting; proof and caregiver permission are unnecessary.

rows.label: Principle
items: Inconsistent history, delayed care, or developmentally impossible mechanism increase suspicion

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Report to child protective services** promptly; urgent danger → emergency protective services
Stabilize; document verbatim statements, findings and photographs; interview caregivers separately
★ Suspected physical abuse age <2 → **skeletal survey**; repeat after approximately 2 weeks

rows.label: Don't
items: Confront or accuse caregivers; promise secrecy; delay reporting for complete diagnostic certainty
Discharge into an unsafe setting; substitute reporting to a supervisor for mandated reporting

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Financial hardship alone ≠ neglect; assess ability to obtain food, shelter and medical care
Consider bleeding disorders, osteogenesis imperfecta and accidental trauma without delaying protection

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Metaphyseal corner/posterior rib fractures**; mixed healing stages → abuse concern
Immersion burns: uniform depth, sharp edges, stocking/glove pattern; nonmobile infants: sentinel bruising
★ Abusive head trauma: acceleration-deceleration tears bridging veins → **subdural, retinal hemorrhages**

table.title: Presentation → evaluation
rows: AST/ALT, lipase, urinalysis; CT if concerning
Growth, nutrition, hygiene, supervision, unmet care needs
Sexual abuse assessment and CPS report

child-abuse-and-neglect.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric safeguarding principles; reporting procedures vary by jurisdiction.

child-growth-and-development.name: Child growth and development
child-growth-and-development.scope: Normal growth velocity, weight doubling and tripling milestones, WHO/CDC growth chart interpretation, developmental surveillance, normal toddler behavioral variants (head banging, temper tantrums)
child-growth-and-development.core: Interpret serial growth and developmental progress against age, family pattern, and corrected gestational age; a trajectory matters more than one percentile.

rows.label: Definition
items: Weight doubles by 4–6 months, triples by 12 months, quadruples near 24 months
Length increases about 25 cm during year 1; prepubertal height velocity about 5–6 cm/year
★ **WHO charts before 2 years; CDC charts from 2 years** in US practice

rows.label: Interpret
items: Nutrition failure: weight falls first; endocrine disease: height slows with preserved/increased weight
★ Falling **2 major percentile channels**, well child → **diet diary, calorie counts** before labs
Correct prematurity through about 2 years; track infant head circumference

rows.label: Use when
items: Developmental surveillance every visit; standardized general screens at 9, 18, and 30 months
★ **Regression/missed milestones → early intervention**; language delay → **audiometry** before speech testing
BMI-for-age from 2 years; weight-for-length younger; consider parental heights and pubertal timing

rows.label: Compare
items: Tantrums, picky eating, bedtime separation distress → reassure, routines, calm limits; no sedatives
Head banging at sleep onset or frustration, normal development → self-soothing; assess injuries
Preschool restlessness, good function → no stimulants; overwhelmed parent → **parenting classes**

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **One percentile cannot diagnose disease**; stable tracking + normal exam → reassure
Persistent skill loss needs evaluation; never wait for school failure
Short parents, normal bone age → familial; average parents, delayed puberty → **constitutional delay**

rows.label: Adolescence
items: ★ Moodiness, privacy, family detachment, rule-questioning, late bedtimes, good function → reassure, educate parents
Parental-pressure conflict, occasional experimentation, no impairment → not ODD, substance use disorder
Weight worry, stable percentile, normal BMI, regular menses → normal; not eating disorder

table.title: Normal by age
rows: Holds head up; not yet reaching
Sits unsupported; bangs blocks, self-feeds finger foods
Walks; scribbles; non-walker at 14 months normal
Balances on one foot; copies circle
Same-sex parent preference; involve other parent otherwise

child-growth-and-development.evidence: Checked screening ages 2026-10-30: [AAP surveillance/screening](https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/developmental-surveillance-and-screening-patient-care/); growth facts established pediatric teaching.

childhood-and-adolescent-immunizations.name: Childhood and adolescent immunizations
childhood-and-adolescent-immunizations.scope: Routine pediatric vaccine schedule, adolescent immunizations (meningococcal conjugate, HPV, Tdap), catch-up vaccination guidelines
childhood-and-adolescent-immunizations.core: Vaccinate before exposure; use age, prior doses, minimum intervals, and immune status to choose the next dose.

rows.label: Who
items: All children; AAP 2026 schedule retains broad routine childhood protection

rows.label: Schedule
items: ★ 11–12 years: **Tdap, MenACWY**; MenACWY booster at 16 years
AAP HPV: start 9–12 years; <15 years → two doses, 6–12 months apart
HPV initiation ≥15 years or immunocompromised → three doses at 0, 1–2, 6 months

rows.label: Special groups
items: ★ Catch-up: **never restart**; respect minimum ages and intervals
Asplenia/complement defects: extra meningococcal/pneumococcal doses; annual influenza from 6 months
HBsAg-positive mother: HepB vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours of birth

rows.label: Choice
items: MenB: shared decision, usually 16–23 years; high-risk patients need earlier protection

rows.label: Contraindications
items: ★ Live vaccines: pregnancy, severe immunodeficiency; **conjugates (Hib) still indicated**; prior anaphylaxis: no repeat
Rotavirus: SCID, prior intussusception; first dose ≤14 weeks 6 days; finish by 8 months

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **AAP/classic boards: multidose HPV**; federal 2026 policy: one dose
Preterm → **chronological age, full dose**; mild illness, antibiotics, breastfeeding → vaccinate
Separate injectable live vaccines ≥4 weeks unless simultaneous; IVIG can delay MMR/varicella

table.title: Routine AAP childhood schedule
rows: First vaccination <9 years: two ≥4 weeks apart

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
VSD: harsh holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur; ASD: **fixed split S2**, pulmonic flow murmur, RV volume overload
PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses; coarctation: weak femoral pulses, arm–leg BP gradient
Central cyanosis: blue lips/tongue, warm extremities → **low arterial saturation**; peripheral: cold extremities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Left-to-right shunts (VSD, ASD, extracardiac PDA) increase pulmonary flow; remodeling can reverse flow → Eisenmenger syndrome
Duct-dependent lesions require pulmonary/systemic flow or mixing through fetal communications
High neonatal PVR limits VSD shunt → murmur appears/louder over weeks as **PVR falls**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Preductal/right-hand and postductal/foot oxygen saturation; **echocardiography** defines anatomy
★ Hyperoxia test: little PaO2 rise with 100% oxygen suggests cardiac shunting; echo preferred
ECG and chest radiograph support diagnosis; normal murmur does not exclude critical disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected duct-dependent lesion → **prostaglandin E1** immediately; monitor for apnea
★ Tet spell (agitation, softer murmur) → knee–chest, oxygen, fluids, morphine; refractory → phenylephrine or propranolol
TGA with inadequate mixing → balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch
Large shunts → diuretics, closure; premature PDA → ibuprofen; **obstructed TAPVR → emergency repair**
Coarctation → repair; post-repair paradoxical hypertension → **IV beta-blocker**; Eisenmenger → **do not close shunt**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis
Right-to-left shunting → brain abscess, paradoxical emboli, secondary erythrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulse-ox newborn screening; rubella immunization before pregnancy; maternal glycemic control
Endocarditis prophylaxis for selected unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-material lesions during dental procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung disease: substantial oxygen response, pulmonary findings
PPHN: elevated pulmonary resistance with structurally normal heart

table.title: Five cyanotic lesions
rows: RV obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH; boot-shaped heart
Parallel circuits; single S2; egg-on-string silhouette
Pulmonary veins drain systemically; obstruction → edema

congenital-heart-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric cardiology teaching.

congenital-infections.name: Congenital infections
congenital-infections.scope: Cytomegalovirus (sensorineural hearing loss, periventricular calcifications), Toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis), Parvovirus B19 (hydrops), Rubella, Varicella, Zika, screening and diagnosis
congenital-infections.core: Congenital infection causes growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, or hydrops; organ-specific patterns identify the pathogen.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: CMV: toddler saliva/urine; toxoplasma: undercooked meat, cat feces; B19: child with slapped-cheek rash
Absent rubella/varicella immunity; mosquito exposure or sexual transmission in Zika-risk areas

rows.label: Clues
items: Petechiae/blueberry-muffin lesions, abnormal fetal ultrasound; many infected newborns initially appear well
★ B19 hydrops: cardiomegaly, ascites, edema without red-cell alloantibodies
Maternal rash: B19 → slapped cheek, then reticular limb rash; rubella → descending rash, postauricular nodes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transplacental infection disrupts organogenesis; later exposure may cause inflammation or marrow suppression
Toxoplasma transmission increases with gestational age; earlier infection causes more severe injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Maternal exposure → pathogen-specific **IgG/IgM**, paired titers or avidity; isolated IgM needs confirmation
★ CMV newborn diagnosis: saliva PCR then confirm urine PCR **within 21 days**
Suspected fetal infection → targeted ultrasound, pathogen-specific amniotic-fluid PCR; B19 → serial MCA Doppler
Prenatal rubella IgG routinely; no universal US maternal CMV, toxoplasma, or B19 screening

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic congenital CMV → **valganciclovir**, monitor CBC and liver tests
Congenital toxoplasmosis → pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin; maternal regimen depends on fetal infection
B19 severe fetal anemia → intrauterine transfusion; rubella/Zika structural injury → supportive care
Maternal varicella exposure without immunity → varicella-zoster immune globulin; maternal pneumonia → IV acyclovir
Maternal varicella onset 5 days before to 2 days after delivery → **newborn VZIG**

rows.label: Complications
items: Stillbirth, neurodevelopmental disability; delayed/progressive hearing loss requires longitudinal audiology

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Rubella/varicella vaccination before pregnancy or postpartum; **live vaccines contraindicated during pregnancy**
Handwashing after diapers; cook meat, avoid litter handling; mosquito precautions and Zika exposure counseling
Term newborn of varicella-immune mother: transplacental IgG protects → no prophylaxis after exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aneuploidy: abnormal genetic testing rather than pathogen testing
Rh disease: positive maternal antibody screen with fetal anemia

table.title: Discriminating congenital patterns
rows: Periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, chorioretinitis
Severe microcephaly, subcortical calcifications, ocular abnormalities

congenital-infections.evidence: CMV testing checked 2026-10-30: [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/cytomegalovirus/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html); remaining pathogen patterns established teaching.

congenital-urinary-tract-anomalies.name: Congenital urinary tract anomalies
congenital-urinary-tract-anomalies.scope: Posterior urethral valves (oligohydramnios, palpable bladder, VCUG, ablation), vesicoureteral reflux (hydronephrosis, recurrent UTI), ureteropelvic junction obstruction, cryptorchidism, hypospadias
congenital-urinary-tract-anomalies.core: Prenatal collecting-system dilation, recurrent febrile UTI, or abnormal genital examination requires localization of obstruction, reflux, or disordered development.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Posterior urethral valves occur only in boys; reflux may cluster in families
Cryptorchidism: prematurity, low birth weight; hypospadias: disrupted urethral development

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Boy with **weak stream, palpable bladder**, bilateral hydronephrosis → outlet obstruction
Severe fetal obstruction → oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, Potter sequence
Recurrent febrile UTIs, poor growth, hypertension may signal reflux nephropathy
★ Hypospadias + bilateral nonpalpable testes → urgent disorder-of-sex-development evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: High urinary pressure or retrograde infected urine damages developing renal parenchyma
Undescended testes experience thermal injury; ectopic ventral meatus may accompany chordee

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Renal/bladder **ultrasound** first; creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis/culture assess consequences
VCUG after abnormal ultrasound suggesting reflux/obstruction or recurrent febrile UTIs; not every first uncomplicated UTI
UPJ dilation without hydroureter → MAG3 diuretic renography for drainage and differential function
Cryptorchidism: examination; no pre-referral ultrasound; bilateral nonpalpable testes → endocrine/genetic evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Valves: bladder catheter decompression, correct fluids/electrolytes → endoscopic **valve ablation**
Reflux: low-risk → observation; high-risk → consider TMP-SMX prophylaxis; breakthrough febrile UTIs → ureteral reimplantation
UPJ obstruction: observe preserved function; worsening drainage/function or symptoms → pyeloplasty
Cryptorchidism: refer at 6 months corrected age; orchiopexy by 18 months
★ Hypospadias: **defer circumcision**; foreskin may support reconstruction; repair generally 6–18 months

rows.label: Complications
items: Renal scarring, CKD, hypertension; valve bladder dysfunction may persist after successful ablation
Cryptorchidism: subfertility, torsion, malignancy; orchiopexy reduces but does not eliminate cancer risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat constipation and dysfunctional voiding to reduce recurrent UTIs
Prompt fever evaluation and long-term BP/renal-function surveillance after significant reflux or obstruction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Retractile testis: can remain in scrotum after manipulation; monitor annually for ascent
Physiologic neonatal dilation: resolves without progressive functional loss

cystic-fibrosis.name: Cystic fibrosis
cystic-fibrosis.scope: CFTR mutations, meconium ileus, bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, sweat chloride test
cystic-fibrosis.core: Recurrent sinopulmonary infection plus malabsorption, poor growth or neonatal meconium ileus suggests CFTR dysfunction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autosomal recessive CFTR variants; affected sibling or carrier parents
F508del is common; genotype determines eligibility for specific CFTR modulators

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic productive cough, recurrent pneumonia, nasal polyps, clubbing and bronchiectasis
Greasy stools, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, failure to thrive despite appetite
Salty skin, dehydration with hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; male infertility from absent vas deferens
Neonatal abdominal distention with inspissated ileal meconium; later rectal prolapse possible

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Defective apical chloride/bicarbonate transport → dehydrated airway and pancreatic secretions
Sweat ducts fail to reabsorb chloride; pancreatic duct blockage causes exocrine destruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Positive newborn immunoreactive trypsinogen screen → **quantitative sweat chloride** confirmation
★ Sweat chloride **≥60 mmol/L** supports CF; 30–59 intermediate → repeat/genetic evaluation
Two CF-causing variants in trans or specialized CFTR-function testing resolve uncertain cases
Fecal elastase assesses pancreatic insufficiency; sputum cultures guide respiratory antibiotics
Consider CF despite negative limited mutation panel when clinical phenotype is compelling

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Daily **airway clearance**, hypertonic saline, dornase alfa; exercise supports mucus clearance
Pulmonary exacerbation → culture-directed antibiotics; Pseudomonas commonly needs antipseudomonal coverage
★ Pancreatic insufficiency → **pancrelipase with meals**, high-calorie nutrition, vitamins A/D/E/K
Eligible genotype → elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor; check liver function and interactions
Advanced respiratory failure → oxygen/ventilatory support and lung transplant assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Pseudomonas colonization, massive hemoptysis, pneumothorax, respiratory failure
CF-related diabetes, biliary liver disease, distal intestinal obstruction, osteoporosis and infertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Vaccination, nutrition monitoring, salt/fluid replacement during heat or exercise
Infection-control separation between CF patients; family carrier testing and reproductive counseling

rows.label: Mimics
items: Primary ciliary dyskinesia: situs inversus possible; normal pancreatic function/sweat chloride
Immunodeficiency: recurrent infection without CFTR-pattern salt loss
Celiac disease: malabsorption without bronchiectasis

cystic-fibrosis.evidence: Diagnostic threshold checked 2026-10-30: [CF Foundation sweat testing](https://www.cff.org/intro-cf/sweat-test); management established CF teaching.

dysmenorrhea.name: Dysmenorrhea
dysmenorrhea.scope: Primary dysmenorrhea, secondary dysmenorrhea (endometriosis, adenomyosis, cervical stenosis), hematometra, NSAIDs, combined oral contraceptives
dysmenorrhea.core: Painful menstruation: primary disease begins after ovulatory cycles develop; later-onset, progressive, or refractory pain suggests pelvic pathology.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Early menarche, heavy/prolonged flow, family history, smoking
Prior cervical excision/ablation → stenosis; endometriosis and adenomyosis produce secondary symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Suprapubic cramping radiating to back/thighs, nausea, diarrhea, headache
★ **Dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding, infertility**, or pain outside menses → secondary cause
Amenorrhea or scant flow after cervical procedure with cyclic pain → retained menstrual blood

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Progesterone withdrawal → endometrial prostaglandins → uterine hypercontractility and ischemia
Outflow obstruction traps blood in uterine cavity → hematometra

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Classic adolescent presentation without red flags → **clinical diagnosis**, no initial imaging
Sexual activity → pregnancy test; infection risks → gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT
Secondary features → pelvic examination and **transvaginal ultrasound**; transabdominal imaging if needed
No improvement after 3–6 months despite adherence → investigate secondary disease, consider laparoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NSAIDs**, starting 1–2 days before expected bleeding through first 2–3 days
★ Inadequate response/contraception desired → **combined OCP** or progestin; continuous suppression may help
Heat, exercise; avoid NSAIDs with active ulcer disease or significant renal dysfunction
Treat underlying lesion; cervical stenosis with hematometra → cervical dilation/drainage

rows.label: Complications
items: School/work absence, sleep disturbance; untreated secondary disease may impair fertility
Analgesic adverse effects: GI bleeding, renal injury; estrogen-containing contraception → VTE risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Track cycles and preempt pain; ongoing menstrual suppression reduces recurrence when pregnancy not desired

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG, nonmenstrual bleeding, possible instability
PID: fever, mucopurulent discharge, cervical motion tenderness

table.title: Secondary patterns
rows: Posterior nodularity; ultrasound may be normal
Heavy bleeding, boggy uniformly enlarged uterus

dysmenorrhea.evidence: Not checked online; established adolescent gynecology and pelvic-pain teaching.

fetal-alcohol-syndrome.name: Fetal alcohol syndrome
fetal-alcohol-syndrome.scope: Facial dysmorphism (smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, small palpebral fissures), prenatal/postnatal growth restriction, microcephaly, intellectual disability, neurobehavioral deficits, maternal alcohol screening
fetal-alcohol-syndrome.core: A child with growth restriction, characteristic facial features, and persistent central nervous system dysfunction may have prenatal alcohol-related injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prenatal alcohol exposure, especially binge/heavy use; injury possible throughout pregnancy
Maternal alcohol use disorder, limited prenatal care; individual susceptibility and timing modify severity

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Facial pattern: **smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion, short palpebral fissures**; flat nasal bridge possible
Prenatal/postnatal growth deficiency, small head circumference
Executive/attention deficits, poor impulse control, impaired adaptive behavior; intellectual disability variable
Normal intelligence or absent facial features does not exclude broader fetal alcohol spectrum disorder

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alcohol crosses placenta → disrupted neuronal migration, proliferation, survival and craniofacial development

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical multidisciplinary assessment**: growth, dysmorphology, neurodevelopment and prenatal exposure history
Obtain collateral prenatal records sensitively; no laboratory test confirms remote fetal exposure
FAS diagnosis can be possible without confirmed exposure when defining phenotype present; diagnostic systems differ
Evaluate hearing/vision, congenital anomalies and competing genetic diagnoses

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Early developmental intervention**, individualized education, speech/occupational therapy, behavioral supports
Stable structured caregiving, predictable routines, caregiver education; coordinate social services
Treat diagnosed ADHD, mood or sleep disorders individually; no drug reverses prenatal injury
Assess feeding/growth and provide nutritional support; manage congenital heart or other structural disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Lifelong learning/adaptive impairment, mental illness, substance misuse, disrupted schooling and legal difficulties
Cardiac septal defects and other congenital anomalies may coexist

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **No known safe amount or timing of alcohol** during pregnancy or attempted conception
Universal nonjudgmental maternal screening with AUDIT-C/T-ACE; brief intervention and treatment referral
Alcohol dependence → supervised withdrawal/treatment planning; offer contraception counseling when pregnancy not desired

rows.label: Mimics
items: Down syndrome: macroglossia, hypotonia, upslanting fissures; palmar crease, epicanthal folds occur in both
Fragile X: long face, large ears, macroorchidism; no smooth philtrum
Isolated ADHD: no defining growth/facial phenotype; may coexist
Environmental deprivation: developmental deficits without characteristic embryopathy

fetal-alcohol-syndrome.evidence: Prevention checked 2026-10-30: [CDC FASD](https://www.cdc.gov/fasd/about/); established developmental assessment.

gastroenteritis.name: Gastroenteritis
gastroenteritis.scope: Viral gastroenteritis (rotavirus, norovirus), foodborne illness, bacterial enteritis, traveler's diarrhea (ETEC), oral rehydration therapy, dehydration assessment
gastroenteritis.core: Acute vomiting and diarrhea usually need hydration and selective testing; shock, blood, focal pain, or systemic toxicity changes the approach.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sick contacts, contaminated food/water, travel, childcare or institutional outbreaks
Infants, older adults and immunocompromised people have greater dehydration or invasive-infection risk
Pet reptiles → nontyphoidal Salmonella; young infants prone to bacteremia

rows.label: Clues
items: Watery stools and diffuse cramps favor noninvasive disease; fever or dysentery suggests inflammatory enteritis
Mild dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, reduced urine; children → fewer wet diapers, absent tears
★ Lethargy, delayed capillary refill, tachycardia, hypotension → **severe dehydration/shock**
Toddler + high fever, bloody diarrhea, **seizure** → Shigella; HUS appears days later with hemolysis/AKI

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intestinal secretion or epithelial injury causes water/electrolyte losses
Sodium–glucose cotransport remains functional, allowing oral rehydration despite ongoing diarrhea

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Mild self-limited illness → **no routine stool tests**
Stool PCR/culture and Shiga toxin for bloody diarrhea, high fever, severe pain or sepsis
Electrolytes/creatinine for severe dehydration; C difficile testing after antibiotics or healthcare exposure
Persistent >14 days or relevant travel → evaluate parasites; focal/peritoneal pain → imaging for surgical cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Oral rehydration solution**, frequent small volumes; continue breastfeeding and usual diet
Shock/severe dehydration or failed oral intake → IV isotonic crystalloid; reassess perfusion
Ondansetron can enable oral hydration; avoid juice/soda as primary replacement
Moderate/severe travelers’ diarrhea → azithromycin; suspected STEC → no antibiotics
Loperamide only selected adults with afebrile nonbloody diarrhea; avoid children and inflammatory disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Prerenal AKI, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte abnormalities; postinfectious lactose intolerance
STEC → HUS with hemolysis, low platelets and AKI; invasive bacteria → bacteremia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Handwashing with soap/water, food safety, **rotavirus vaccination** in infancy
Norovirus outbreaks: environmental disinfection; food handlers remain off work ≥48 hours after symptoms resolve

rows.label: Mimics
items: Appendicitis/intussusception: localized or episodic severe pain disproportionate to diarrhea
DKA: hyperglycemia, ketones; IBD: persistent bloody diarrhea and weight loss

table.title: Common noninvasive enteritis
rows: Vomiting followed by substantial watery diarrhea

hirsutism.name: Hirsutism
hirsutism.scope: Idiopathic hirsutism, peripheral 5-alpha-reductase overactivity, evaluation of androgen excess, nonclassic CAH, androgen-secreting neoplasms, oral contraceptives, spironolactone
hirsutism.core: Terminal hair in androgen-dependent areas in women requires distinguishing gradual androgen sensitivity/PCOS from rapid virilization due to a secreting tumor.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: PCOS, familial/ethnic hair distribution, nonclassic CAH, exogenous androgens/anabolic steroids
Rare ovarian/adrenal neoplasm; medications causing generalized hypertrichosis differ from androgenic hair growth

rows.label: Clues
items: Facial, chest, lower-abdominal terminal hair; acne and irregular menses favor androgen excess
★ **Rapid progression, deep voice, clitoromegaly**, increased muscle mass → tumor evaluation
Regular ovulatory cycles with normal androgens and slow growth favor idiopathic hirsutism

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Androgens convert vellus to terminal hairs; follicular 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to potent DHT
Idiopathic disease reflects increased peripheral sensitivity despite normal circulating hormones

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Moderate/severe hair growth or endocrine signs → morning **total testosterone**, reliable assay
DHEA-S assesses adrenal source; early-morning follicular **17-hydroxyprogesterone** screens nonclassic CAH
Marked testosterone elevation, often >150–200 ng/dL → pelvic imaging; DHEA-S >700 µg/dL → adrenal imaging
Equivocal 17-hydroxyprogesterone → ACTH stimulation; TSH/prolactin or cortisol testing only for matching features
Mild localized hair without abnormal cycles/endocrine signs often needs no extensive hormone workup

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pregnancy not desired → **combined OCP** first-line; reassess after ≥6 months
★ Persistent symptoms → add **spironolactone with reliable contraception**; monitor potassium/renal function
Shaving, waxing, laser/photoepilation; topical eflornithine slows facial hair growth
Treat tumor/endocrine cause; weight loss benefits metabolic risk and androgen excess in PCOS

rows.label: Complications
items: Psychological distress; spironolactone → hyperkalemia, menstrual irregularity, male fetal undervirilization
Estrogen contraception → VTE risk; avoid when estrogen contraindicated

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid androgen supplements; counsel slow hair-cycle response and ongoing maintenance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypertrichosis: diffuse nonandrogen distribution; minoxidil, phenytoin, cyclosporine
Cushing syndrome: striae, proximal weakness, easy bruising accompany hair changes

hirsutism.evidence: Treatment checked 2026-10-30: [SOGC 444](https://www.sogc.org/common/Uploaded%20files/ACSC/ACSC2024/gui444CPG2312E.pdf); biochemical localization established endocrine teaching.

hordeolum-and-chalazion.name: Hordeolum and chalazion
hordeolum-and-chalazion.scope: External hordeolum (stye), internal hordeolum, chalazion (granulomatous meibomian cyst), blepharitis, warm compresses, incision and curettage
hordeolum-and-chalazion.core: Localized eyelid lump: acute infection versus retained glandular lipid; most resolve with conservative drainage-promoting care.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Blepharitis, meibomian dysfunction, rosacea, poor lid hygiene, recurrent eye rubbing
Recurrent infections → consider diabetes; bacterial lesions usually involve Staphylococcus aureus

rows.label: Clues
items: Blepharitis: crusting at lash bases, gritty/burning eyes, erythematous lid margins
★ **Painful eye movements, proptosis, impaired vision, fever** → orbital cellulitis; emergency evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Obstruction retains secretions; bacterial invasion → abscess; sterile lipid leakage → granulomatous inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: Clinical inspection with lid eversion; uncomplicated localized lesions need no laboratory testing or imaging
★ **Recurrent same-site or atypical lesion → biopsy**, especially older adult or associated lash loss
Diffuse swelling → assess ocular motility, acuity, pupils; suspected orbital disease → contrast orbital CT

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Warm compresses 10–15 minutes, several times daily**, gentle massage, lid cleansing first
Draining stye plus blepharitis → topical erythromycin; sterile lesions need no antibiotics
Spreading preseptal cellulitis → oral amoxicillin-clavulanate; orbital signs → admit, IV antibiotics
★ Persistent/vision-distorting chalazion → **incision and curettage** or intralesional triamcinolone by ophthalmology
Persistent hordeolum abscess → incision/drainage; avoid squeezing, puncturing, contact lenses, and eye makeup

rows.label: Complications
items: Large upper-lid mass → corneal astigmatism, amblyopia risk in children
Infected lesion → preseptal cellulitis; recurrent nodules may obscure underlying malignancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Daily lid hygiene for chronic blepharitis; treat rosacea; remove makeup before sleep
Wash hands and clean contact lenses; avoid sharing eye cosmetics

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sebaceous carcinoma: persistent firm nodule, lash loss, unilateral refractory blepharitis
Dacryocystitis: tender swelling below medial canthus, lacrimal sac location
Preseptal cellulitis: diffuse lid erythema without discrete glandular lump; ocular function preserved

table.title: Lump classification
rows: Infected lash follicle/Zeis or Moll gland
Acute tender pustule at lid margin
Deeper painful swelling; points toward conjunctiva

hyperglycemic-crises.name: Hyperglycemic crises
hyperglycemic-crises.core: Insulin-deficient diabetes with osmotic diuresis: rapid acidotic illness or slowly progressive hyperosmolar encephalopathy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Infection, missed insulin, pump failure, MI; DKA often type 1, HHS often older type 2
Euglycemic triggers: **SGLT2 inhibitors**, pregnancy, fasting

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria, thirst, weight loss, dry mucosa, tachycardia
DKA: abdominal pain, vomiting, **Kussmaul (deep) breathing**; HHS: profound dehydration, focal deficits
★ Severe: **hypotension, stupor**, or coma → ICU

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insulin deficit + counterregulatory hormones → lipolysis, ketogenesis; residual insulin in HHS limits ketosis
Total-body K depleted despite initially normal/high serum K

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose, electrolytes, venous pH, β-hydroxybutyrate**, osmolality; ECG + trigger evaluation
Effective osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose/18; glucose in mg/dL
★ HHS: **effective osmolality >300 OR total >320 mOsm/kg**; substantial ketosis/acidosis → mixed DKA/HHS
DKA resolution: ketones <0.6 mmol/L AND (pH ≥7.3 OR HCO₃ ≥18); urine ketones/anion gap misleading

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IV isotonic crystalloid → K correction → IV regular insulin**; K <3.5 mmol/L → delay insulin
Replace K when <5 mmol/L; glucose checks every 1–2 h, electrolytes/pH/ketones every 4 h
★ Add **dextrose** below glucose 250; euglycemic presentation → immediately; continue insulin until crisis resolves
SC basal insulin overlaps infusion 1–2 h; bicarbonate only consider pH <7.0; HHS: slower osmolar correction

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, thrombosis; treatment: hypoglycemia, hypokalemic arrhythmias, cerebral edema (Cushing triad), hyperchloremic acidosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sick-day fluids/ketone checks; continue basal insulin; ensure supplies and early follow-up
Hold SGLT2 inhibitors during acute illness and before surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcoholic ketoacidosis: binge then poor intake; usually no diabetes
Starvation ketosis: usually milder acidosis, no marked hyperglycemia
Toxic alcohols: osmolar gap, exposure; absent substantial ketonemia

table.title: Biochemistry; ketones and HCO₃ in mmol/L

hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.name: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.scope: infantile presentation (nonbilious projectile vomiting, olive mass), hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, ultrasound diagnosis, fluid resuscitation, pyloromyotomy
hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.core: A hungry young infant with progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting suggests gastric outlet obstruction from pyloric muscle hypertrophy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually 2–8 weeks old; more common in firstborn boys and with family history
Early-life macrolide exposure, especially erythromycin; bottle feeding and maternal smoking associated

rows.label: Clues
items: Vomiting becomes forceful after feeds; dehydration, weight loss, fewer wet diapers
★ **Palpable epigastric/right-upper-quadrant olive**, visible left-to-right gastric peristalsis
★ **Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis** after prolonged vomiting; labs may initially be normal
Bilious emesis is atypical and demands urgent evaluation for obstruction distal to ampulla

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypertrophied pyloric circular muscle obstructs gastric emptying without blocking bile drainage into distal bowel
Gastric HCl loss and contraction activate aldosterone → renal potassium loss; severe depletion causes paradoxical aciduria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ultrasound first**: thickened elongated pylorus with impaired passage
Typical thresholds: muscle thickness ≥3 mm, channel length ≥15 mm; interpret by infant size
Equivocal early study → repeat ultrasound; upper GI series can show string sign if uncertainty persists
Electrolytes, glucose, renal function, blood gas assess resuscitation needs before anesthesia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO + IV isotonic saline**, glucose-containing maintenance fluid; correct chloride deficit first
Replace potassium after confirming urine output; monitor hydration and electrolytes
★ **Pyloromyotomy after normalization** of volume and alkalosis; medical stabilization precedes definitive surgery
NG decompression when ongoing vomiting/distention; postoperative feeds advanced with surgical team

rows.label: Complications
items: Severe dehydration, failure to thrive, prerenal AKI, hypokalemic arrhythmia
Persistent alkalosis increases perioperative apnea risk; surgery can cause mucosal perforation or incomplete myotomy
Brief postoperative emesis can occur; persistent worsening vomiting warrants reassessment

rows.label: Prevention
items: No reliable primary prevention; avoid unnecessary neonatal macrolides, without withholding necessary treatment
Early recognition of progressive vomiting prevents severe electrolyte depletion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Physiologic reflux: effortless small spit-ups, normal growth
Malrotation/volvulus: bilious vomiting, acute illness; urgent upper GI evaluation/surgery
Milk-protein allergy: bloody stools, eczema, feeding intolerance rather than fixed outlet obstruction

hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric surgery teaching.

hypoglycemia.name: Hypoglycemia
hypoglycemia.scope: Drug-induced hypoglycemia (insulin, sulfonylureas), Whipple triad, acute management (dextrose, glucagon), insulinoma
hypoglycemia.core: Compatible symptoms, documented low plasma glucose, and relief with correction establish Whipple triad and justify evaluation for a hypoglycemic disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Insulin, sulfonylureas; missed meals, exercise, alcohol, kidney failure increase risk
Sepsis, liver failure, adrenal insufficiency; insulinoma causes fasting episodes in otherwise well adults
Child, illness, poor intake or sugar-free fluids → **glycogen depletion**, ketotic hypoglycemia ± anion-gap acidosis

rows.label: Clues
items: Adrenergic: tremor, sweating, palpitations, hunger; neuroglycopenic: confusion, visual change, seizures, coma
Autonomic neuropathy or recurrent episodes may blunt warning symptoms
★ Glucose **<54 mg/dL** clinically significant; diabetes alert threshold <70 mg/dL

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Excess insulin suppresses glucose output and ketones; substrate/hormone deficits impair counterregulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside glucose immediately**; plasma confirmation if discordant, never delay emergency correction
Critical sample: glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, β-hydroxybutyrate, sulfonylurea screen
Suspected endogenous fasting disorder → supervised fast up to 72 h; mixed-meal test for postprandial symptoms
Biochemically confirmed insulinoma → pancreatic CT/MRI, endoscopic ultrasound if localization unclear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Awake and swallowing → **15 g rapid carbohydrate**, recheck after 15 minutes, repeat if needed
★ Altered or unable to swallow → **IV dextrose**; no IV access → IM/intranasal glucagon
After recovery → longer-acting carbohydrate; glucagon less effective after alcohol or glycogen depletion
★ Sulfonylurea recurrence → **octreotide + dextrose**, prolonged observation; long-acting insulin may require infusion
Adjust diabetes regimen and treat trigger; localized insulinoma → surgical resection

rows.label: Complications
items: Seizures, brain injury, arrhythmias, falls; recurrent episodes cause impaired awareness
Dextrose alone after sulfonylurea exposure may stimulate further insulin release

rows.label: Prevention
items: Meal/exercise planning, glucose monitoring or CGM alarms, caregiver rescue-glucagon education
Relax overly intensive targets when recurrent events, frailty, or impaired awareness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic attack: normal glucose during symptoms
Stroke: focal deficit may persist after glucose correction; evaluate both if unresolved

hypoglycemia.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine diagnostic and hypoglycemia treatment principles.

hyponatremia.name: Hyponatremia
hyponatremia.scope: Hypovolemic, euvolemic (SIADH, primary polydipsia), hypervolemic, acute vs chronic, hypertonic saline indications
hyponatremia.core: Low serum sodium reflects excess water relative to sodium; symptoms and duration determine urgency before the cause determines maintenance treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, oxytocin; **hypotonic IV D5W**, postoperative state, exercise + excess water
Pulmonary/CNS disease; **small cell lung cancer** (ectopic ADH); heart failure, cirrhosis, renal failure

rows.label: Clues
items: Nausea, headache, gait instability; seizures, coma or marked confusion indicate severe cerebral edema
Orthostasis/dry mucosa suggest depletion; edema/ascites suggest excess extracellular fluid
SIADH: clinically euvolemic with inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypo-osmolality
Massive water intake, often psychiatric illness; urine osmolality below serum still favors polydipsia, even if >100

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into brain; chronic adaptation makes rapid correction dangerous
ADH-mediated water retention or intake exceeding renal dilution capacity lowers sodium concentration
Low effective volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, diarrhea) → baroreceptor ADH release; total-body sodium high in edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serum osmolality first: **<275 mOsm/kg** confirms hypotonicity; assess glucose and volume status
Hyperglycemia → translocational hyponatremia; severe hyperlipidemia/proteinemia → pseudohyponatremia
★ Urine osmolality **<100** → polydipsia/low solute; ≥100 → persistent ADH activity
Urine Na <20–30 suggests low effective arterial volume; >30 suggests renal loss or SIADH
Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and renal failure before diagnosing SIADH; diuretics confound urine Na

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe neurologic symptoms → **3% saline bolus**, repeated for initial Na rise 4–6 mEq/L
Hypovolemia → isotonic saline; SIADH → fluid restriction, increased solute, remove trigger
Edematous states → fluid/sodium restriction and loop diuretic; treat heart/liver/kidney disorder
★ Chronic/unknown duration: generally limit rise to **≤8 mEq/L per 24 h**; monitor frequently
Overcorrection → desmopressin plus D5W; avoid routine vaptans in acute symptomatic cases

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute severe hyponatremia → herniation, respiratory arrest
Osmotic demyelination after rapid correction; greatest risk with alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids during high ADH states; review causative drugs
Monitor for brisk aquaresis after restoring volume or stopping thiazides

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cerebral salt wasting: neurosurgical patient, hypovolemic, high urine Na; SIADH euvolemic
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemia: measured osmolality elevated
Primary psychiatric disease: neurologic change without sodium abnormality

hyponatremia.evidence: Not checked online; established hyponatremia consensus principles.

infant-nutrition.name: Infant nutrition
infant-nutrition.scope: Exclusive breastfeeding recommendations, vitamin D supplementation, introduction of solid foods, cow milk protein allergy (hydrolyzed formula), formula types
infant-nutrition.core: Breast milk or iron-fortified infant formula anchors first-year nutrition; add supplements and complementary foods according to developmental readiness.

rows.label: Who
items: All infants; assess growth, feeding effectiveness, urine output, and family feeding preferences

rows.label: Schedule
items: ★ **Exclusive breastfeeding about 6 months**; continue with complementary foods through 2 years or longer
★ Solids around **6 months**, never before 4; head control, sitting, diminished extrusion reflex
Begin iron-rich meat or fortified cereal; advance textures; introduce allergens without unnecessary delay

rows.label: Special groups
items: ★ Breastfed/partially breastfed → **vitamin D 400 IU/day** from shortly after birth
Formula-only: vitamin D supplement until intake ≥32 oz/day
Exclusively breastfed term infants: **iron 1 mg/kg/day from 4 months** until adequate dietary iron

rows.label: Choice
items: Blood-streaked stool, eczema, emesis → milk-protein allergy; confirm elimination/rechallenge
Breastfed proctocolitis → maternal dairy elimination, dietitian; persistent symptoms → eliminate soy
Proctocolitis: non-IgE, usually outgrown by age 1–3; lactose intolerance: no bloody stool

rows.label: Contraindications
items: No **honey before 12 months**; avoid choking hazards and unpasteurized foods
No cow milk as primary drink before 12 months; no homemade/diluted formula
Classic galactosemia → avoid breast milk and lactose-containing formula

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Lactose-free ≠ hypoallergenic**; avoid partial hydrolysates/goat milk for milk-protein allergy
Severe eczema/egg allergy → peanut evaluation and introduction at 4–6 months
No cereal in bottles; responsive feeding, no forced finishing

inherited-bleeding-disorders.name: Inherited bleeding disorders
inherited-bleeding-disorders.scope: Hemophilia A, Hemophilia B, von Willebrand disease, factor XI deficiency, hemarthrosis, mixing studies, factor VIII inhibitors
inherited-bleeding-disorders.core: Deep tissue bleeding suggests a coagulation-factor defect; mucosal bleeding suggests platelet/von Willebrand dysfunction, even with a normal platelet count.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemophilia A/B: X-linked, usually males; maternal family history may be absent
vWD usually autosomal dominant; factor XI deficiency autosomal, enriched in Ashkenazi ancestry

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Recurrent **hemarthroses**, muscle hematomas and delayed postoperative bleeding → hemophilia
Epistaxis, gingival bleeding, easy bruising and heavy menses → vWD
Factor XI deficiency: variable postsurgical bleeding, especially oral/urologic procedures; hemarthrosis uncommon
Unexpected major bleeding after circumcision or surgery may reveal previously undiagnosed disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: VIII/IX/XI deficits impair intrinsic-pathway thrombin generation and fibrin stabilization
vWF mediates platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII; deficiency impairs primary and sometimes secondary hemostasis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ CBC/platelets, PT, aPTT; **mixing study corrects** factor deficiency, fails with inhibitor
Factor VIII, IX or XI activity identifies deficiency; hemophilia generally normal PT/platelets
★ Suspected vWD → **vWF antigen, activity and factor VIII**; aPTT may be normal
Stress, pregnancy and estrogen raise vWF; repeat borderline testing when clinically stable
Severe hemophilia: factor activity <1%; inhibitor testing if replacement response is inadequate

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Major suspected hemophilic bleeding → **replace deficient factor immediately**, before imaging delays
Hemophilia A → factor VIII; B → factor IX; emicizumab prophylaxis for selected A
Mild responsive A or type 1 vWD → **desmopressin after response testing**
Severe vWD → vWF-containing concentrate; avoid desmopressin in type 2B and ineffective type 3
Mucosal bleeding → tranexamic acid; factor XI procedures → antifibrinolytic ± plasma with hematology planning

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic hemarthropathy, intracranial hemorrhage, anemia; factor inhibitors complicate replacement
Desmopressin → water retention/hyponatremia; factor concentrates can increase thrombosis risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Individualized factor/nonfactor prophylaxis, dental care, procedure planning; avoid aspirin and nonselective NSAIDs
Family genetic counseling; fluid restriction and sodium monitoring around desmopressin

rows.label: Mimics
items: ITP: low platelets with mucocutaneous bleeding
Acquired factor VIII inhibitor: new bleeding, mixing fails to correct
Vitamin K deficiency: PT prolonged first

innocent-murmurs.name: Innocent murmurs
innocent-murmurs.scope: Still murmur, venous hum, physiologic peripheral pulmonary stenosis, pulmonary flow murmur, benign vs pathologic features, reassurance
innocent-murmurs.core: Incidental flow sound in an otherwise healthy child; distinguish normal hemodynamics from structural heart disease using examination and positional maneuvers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Childhood; fever, anemia, exercise, anxiety → increased flow and audibility
Prematurity favors physiologic branch pulmonary artery narrowing

rows.label: Clues
items: Soft, localized, short systolic sound; normal pulses, growth, oxygenation, S2; no thrill
★ **Diastolic, holosystolic, harsh, or ≥grade 3** → evaluate for pathology
★ Exertional syncope, chest pain, cyanosis, poor feeding, or growth failure → **cardiology referral**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Normal blood-flow vibrations without valve dysfunction, shunting, or chamber pressure overload

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Auscultation supine and standing**; assess femoral pulses, BP, family sudden-death history
Classic benign examination in older child → clinical diagnosis; routine ECG/CXR add little
Uncertain findings or persistent neonatal murmur → pediatric cardiology; **echocardiography** defines structural lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reassurance**; unrestricted sports and usual childhood activities
No cardiac drugs, endocarditis prophylaxis, or serial imaging after confident benign diagnosis

rows.label: Complications
items: No heart failure or progression to structural disease; mistaken labeling → anxiety and unnecessary activity restriction

rows.label: Mimics
items: ASD: fixed split S2; pulmonary stenosis: ejection click
PDA: unvarying machinery sound; bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: louder with standing or Valsalva; concerning family history

table.title: Benign patterns
rows: Disappears supine or with jugular compression

intussusception.name: Intussusception
intussusception.scope: Idiopathic ileocolic intussusception, pathologic lead points (Meckel, polyp), target sign on ultrasound, air enema
intussusception.core: Bowel telescoping causes intermittent obstruction and ischemia, often in a previously healthy infant with episodic distress and deceptively well intervals.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually age 6–36 months; lymphoid hyperplasia after viral illness
Older child, recurrent episode or adult → pathologic lead point: Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Sudden recurrent **colicky pain with knees drawn up**, pallor and vomiting
Lethargy/pallor between spasms can mimic neurologic illness; bilious emesis or distention suggests progressing obstruction
Sausage-shaped RUQ mass, empty RLQ; currant-jelly stool is late and often absent
Shock, guarding, fever or peritonitis → compromised bowel/perforation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Proximal bowel and mesentery invaginate distally → venous congestion, edema and arterial ischemia
Ileocolic location most common in children; bleeding reflects injured mucosa

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound first** → target/doughnut on transverse view, pseudokidney longitudinally
Plain radiograph for obstruction/free air when severe findings; normal radiograph does not exclude
CT generally for adult cases or uncertain alternative diagnosis, not routine pediatric first test
Classic clinical triad uncommon; do not delay testing until bloody stools appear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV fluids**, analgesia; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Stable without peritonitis/perforation → **air or contrast enema**: diagnostic and therapeutic, surgical backup
Failed reduction, perforation, shock or peritonitis → urgent surgery; resect nonviable bowel
Persistent/recurrent disease or suspected lead point → surgical evaluation; adult cases usually require resection

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, shock; recurrence after successful reduction
Enema-associated perforation → immediate surgical management

rows.label: Prevention
items: No usual primary prevention for idiopathic disease; remove identified pathologic lead point
After reduction → observe recovery, resume intake when tolerated; counsel on recurrent episodic symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: diarrhea predominates, less discrete symptom-free intervals
Malrotation/volvulus: bilious vomiting in neonate, urgent surgical evaluation
Meckel bleed or juvenile polyp: painless rectal bleeding, no colicky episodes

neonatal-respiratory-distress.name: Neonatal respiratory distress
neonatal-respiratory-distress.scope: Transient tachypnea of the newborn, respiratory distress syndrome, meconium aspiration syndrome, persistent PH
neonatal-respiratory-distress.core: Tachypnea, retractions, grunting, or cyanosis after birth requires stabilization while gestational age, delivery history, and imaging narrow the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prematurity/maternal diabetes → RDS; cesarean without labor → TTN; post-term/meconium → aspiration
Maternal fever, prolonged membrane rupture or inadequate GBS prophylaxis raise concern for infectious pneumonia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Apnea, bradycardia, poor perfusion or severe hypoxemia** → immediate neonatal resuscitation
PPHN: labile hypoxemia, preductal right-hand saturation higher than postductal foot saturation
Unilateral absent breath sounds or abrupt deterioration → pneumothorax; scaphoid abdomen → diaphragmatic hernia
TTN improves within 24–72 hours; persistent/worsening disease warrants reassessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Poor lung expansion, airway obstruction or V/Q mismatch impairs oxygenation
PPHN: persistently high pulmonary resistance causes right-to-left ductal/atrial shunting

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pulse oximetry, blood gas and chest radiograph** after initial stabilization
Pre/postductal saturation comparison and echocardiography for suspected PPHN; exclude structural heart disease
Possible infection → blood culture and CBC; biomarkers cannot independently exclude sepsis
Persistent unexplained hypoxemia → echocardiography rather than assuming primary pulmonary disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Warmth, oxygen titrated to neonatal targets; **CPAP** for breathing infant with distress
Apnea/gasping or HR <100 → positive-pressure ventilation; ineffective ventilation requires corrective steps/advanced airway
RDS with increasing oxygen need → intratracheal surfactant; mechanical ventilation if noninvasive support fails
★ PPHN → lung recruitment/oxygenation, **inhaled nitric oxide** for suitable term/near-term infants; refractory → ECMO
Meconium: no routine tracheal suction; suction only obstructed ventilation; suspected sepsis → ampicillin/gentamicin

rows.label: Complications
items: Air leak, hypoxic brain injury, death; prematurity/ventilation → bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Antenatal corticosteroids when preterm delivery expected; avoid elective delivery before 39 weeks
Treat maternal infection, provide indicated intrapartum GBS prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cyanotic congenital heart disease: abnormal cardiac anatomy on echo
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: bowel in chest; intubate and decompress stomach, avoid bag-mask ventilation

table.title: Lung patterns
rows: Low volumes, diffuse ground glass/air bronchograms
May be normal or reflect trigger

neonatal-sepsis.name: Neonatal sepsis
neonatal-sepsis.scope: Early-onset neonatal sepsis, late-onset neonatal sepsis, Group B Streptococcus, Listeria, ampicillin and gentamicin
neonatal-sepsis.core: A newborn with temperature instability, feeding difficulty, apnea, or unexplained deterioration may have invasive infection despite subtle examination findings.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Prematurity, maternal GBS, membrane rupture ≥18 hours**, intra-amniotic infection
Late disease: central lines, ventilation, prolonged hospitalization, disrupted skin/GI barriers

rows.label: Clues
items: Hypothermia or fever, lethargy, irritability, poor suck, jaundice, vomiting or glucose instability
Respiratory distress, desaturation, mottling, delayed capillary refill; hypotension is a late sign
Bulging fontanelle or seizures suggest meningitis; vesicles, hepatitis or maternal HSV suggest herpes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immature innate/adaptive immunity permits rapid hematogenous spread
Maternal genital organisms seed early disease; later acquisition includes community and healthcare organisms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Ill neonate → **blood culture before antibiotics**, CBC and inflammatory markers as adjuncts
LP when safe for suspected meningitis, positive blood culture, critical illness or poor response
Urine culture useful in late-onset evaluation; not routinely needed for immediate early-onset disease
Never delay antibiotics for LP in instability; normal WBC/CRP does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early-onset empiric treatment → **ampicillin + gentamicin** after cultures
Suspected meningitis → ampicillin plus cefotaxime where available, tailored to local resistance and cultures
NICU late-onset disease → antistaphylococcal plus gram-negative coverage; vancomycin when MRSA/line resistance risk
★ HSV concern → **IV acyclovir** plus HSV testing; avoid ceftriaxone in neonates
Respiratory/perfusion support; if cultures negative and infant well, stop empiric antibiotics at 36–48 hours

rows.label: Complications
items: Septic shock, DIC, meningitis, hearing loss, neurodevelopmental injury or death
Gentamicin → renal/ototoxicity; unnecessary antibiotics alter microbiome and increase resistant infection risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Maternal **GBS screening and intrapartum penicillin** for positive/eligible high-risk mothers
Hand/line hygiene; well exposed infants ≥35 weeks → serial exams or sepsis-risk calculator strategy

rows.label: Mimics
items: RDS/TTN: delivery-related respiratory pattern without systemic infection evidence
Hypoglycemia or duct-dependent cardiac disease: metabolic/cardiac testing identifies cause

table.title: Common organisms
rows: GBS (most common), E coli; less often Listeria
Coagulase-negative staphylococci, S aureus, gram-negatives, Candida
GBS, E coli, other enteric bacteria

nocturnal-enuresis.name: Nocturnal enuresis
