nocturnal-enuresis.scope: Primary vs secondary nocturnal enuresis, behavioral modifications, enuresis alarm, desmopressin, secondary etiology workup
nocturnal-enuresis.core: Repeated nighttime wetting after age 5; distinguish isolated developmental bedwetting from new wetting caused by urinary, sleep, metabolic, or psychosocial disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, delayed bladder maturation, constipation, sleep-disordered breathing
Secondary episodes may follow stress, diabetes, UTI, or new neurologic disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Primary: never dry ≥6 months; secondary: recurrence after ≥6 months dry
Monosymptomatic: no daytime lower urinary symptoms; urgency, weak stream, or daytime leakage changes evaluation
★ Polydipsia, weight loss, continuous dribbling, recurrent UTIs, abnormal gait → **secondary pathology**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nighttime polyuria, reduced functional bladder capacity, and impaired arousal may coexist
Rectal stool burden worsens bladder function; involuntary wetting is not defiance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **History, growth/BP, abdominal/spinal/neurologic examination + urinalysis**; chart voiding, stools, wet nights
Urine glucose for diabetes concern; pyuria/symptoms → urine culture; assess snoring/apnea
Typical primary monosymptomatic disease needs no imaging, urodynamics, or invasive testing
Daytime symptoms, recurrent febrile UTI, continuous leakage, abnormal examination → ultrasound and specialist evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reassurance, regular daytime voiding, bedtime void**, adequate daytime fluids; reduce evening drinks/caffeine
Treat constipation and daytime urinary dysfunction first; reward participation rather than dry nights
★ **Enuresis alarm** for motivated family seeking durable improvement; requires consistent use over weeks
★ **Desmopressin** for rapid short-term control or alarm failure; recurrence common after stopping
Restrict fluids from 1 h before to 8 h after desmopressin; hold during vomiting/diarrhea illness

rows.label: Complications
items: Embarrassment, low self-esteem, avoidance of sleepovers, family conflict
Desmopressin + excess free water → hyponatremia/seizure; imipramine → potentially fatal cardiotoxicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: Supportive toileting routines and early constipation treatment; never punish or shame
Periodic treatment breaks assess spontaneous maturation; school/social planning preserves confidence

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic ureter: continuous leakage despite normal voids
Diabetes mellitus: polyuria, thirst, glycosuria
UTI: dysuria, frequency, positive culture

nocturnal-enuresis.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric continence and desmopressin safety teaching.

pediatric-exanthems.name: Pediatric exanthems
pediatric-exanthems.scope: Measles (rubeola), rubella (German measles), roseola infantum (HHV-6), erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19 fifth disease), scarlet fever, varicella, clinical appearance, complications
pediatric-exanthems.core: Fever with a childhood rash: use fever timing, rash progression, mucosal findings, immunization status, and pregnancy exposure to distinguish causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Incomplete immunization, daycare/school exposure, travel; immunosuppression increases severe viral disease
Pregnant contacts require prompt assessment after rubella, parvovirus, or varicella exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Toxic appearance**, petechiae/purpura, hypotension, meningismus → evaluate invasive infection immediately
Measles: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis precede rash; rubella: posterior auricular/suboccipital adenopathy
Varicella: trunk/scalp predominance; oral mucosal lesions may accompany the skin eruption

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Parvovirus suppresses erythroid precursors; congenital infection can cause severe fetal anemia
VZV remains latent in sensory ganglia; HHV-6 commonly causes febrile illness in infants

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected measles → **airborne isolation**, notify public health; respiratory PCR plus serum IgM
Scarlet fever → rapid GAS test; negative pediatric test → throat culture
Typical roseola/fifth disease: clinical; atypical vesicles → VZV PCR; rubella → public-health serology/PCR

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Scarlet fever → **penicillin or amoxicillin**; other uncomplicated exanthems generally supportive
Measles → hydration, complication care, clinician-supervised vitamin A for children
Severe/immunocompromised varicella → **IV acyclovir**; avoid aspirin in children

rows.label: Complications
items: Measles: pneumonia, encephalitis, delayed SSPE; rubella: congenital cataracts, deafness, PDA
Parvovirus: aplastic crisis, hydrops, adult symmetric polyarthritis → NSAIDs, not steroids; roseola: febrile seizures
Varicella: bacterial superinfection, pneumonia, cerebellitis; GAS: rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **MMR and varicella vaccines**; live vaccines contraindicated during pregnancy and severe immunosuppression
Measles exposure: MMR within 72 hours or immune globulin within 6 days for eligible contacts

rows.label: Mimics
items: Kawasaki disease: ≥5 days fever, conjunctivitis, oral/extremity changes
Drug eruption: medication exposure without characteristic infectious sequence

table.title: Signature rash
rows: Koplik spots; face → downward confluent rash
Sandpaper rash, Pastia lines, strawberry tongue

pediatric-hip-disorders.name: Pediatric hip disorders
pediatric-hip-disorders.scope: Developmental dysplasia of the hip, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, transient synovitis, pediatric limp workup
pediatric-hip-disorders.core: A child’s limp or knee pain may originate in the hip; age, weight-bearing ability, and hip rotation separate common developmental disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Breech presentation, female sex, family history → developmental hip dysplasia
Obesity and adolescence → slipped capital femoral epiphysis; atypically young/thin cases suggest endocrine disease
Recent viral illness → transient synovitis; Perthes often boys aged 4–8 years

rows.label: Clues
items: Infant asymmetric abduction or leg length; older child limp, groin/thigh/knee pain
★ **Fever, toxic appearance, refusal to bear weight**, painful restricted motion → septic arthritis concern
SCFE: obligate external rotation with flexion, limited internal rotation/abduction; Perthes: gradual painless/painful limp with limited internal rotation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysplasia: shallow acetabulum and unstable femoral head; Perthes: femoral-head avascular necrosis
SCFE: physeal failure displaces epiphysis relative to neck; synovitis: transient sterile joint inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Examine hip in unexplained knee pain**: gait, rotation, fever; limited rotation → **hip x-ray**, not knee MRI
DDH: Ortolani reduces dislocation; Barlow provokes instability; limited abduction more useful after early infancy
Risk-based DDH imaging → ultrasound around 6 weeks; radiograph after femoral ossification, usually ≥4–6 months
Suspected septic hip → CBC, ESR/CRP, cultures, ultrasound for effusion → urgent aspiration
Kocher features: fever >38.5°C, nonweight-bearing, WBC >12,000, ESR >40; support concern, never replace aspiration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected SCFE → **immediate nonweight-bearing**, orthopedic fixation; no forceful manipulation
★ Septic joint → **urgent drainage + IV antibiotics** after cultures when feasible
Transient synovitis → rest, NSAID, close reassessment; persistent/worsening symptoms require renewed evaluation
Perthes → orthopedic containment/ROM plan; DDH treatment depends on age and stability below

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated dysplasia → early osteoarthritis; SCFE → avascular necrosis/chondrolysis
Perthes → femoral-head deformity; missed septic arthritis → irreversible joint destruction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Newborn and infant hip examinations; avoid tight swaddling with extended adducted hips

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: focal bony tenderness, MRI marrow changes
Trauma: injury history and fracture imaging

table.title: Imaging and definitive branch
rows: Sclerosis, flattening, fragmentation; decreased bone-scan uptake

pediatric-hip-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric orthopedic assessment principles.

pneumonia.name: Pneumonia
pneumonia.scope: Community-acquired, hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated, aspiration, atypical pneumonia (Legionella, Mycoplasma)
pneumonia.core: Acute lower respiratory infection with a new infiltrate; severity, acquisition setting, and resistance risks determine disposition and empiric antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, COPD, age, immunosuppression
Dysphagia, absent gag/cough (stroke, dementia, Parkinson), impaired consciousness → aspiration
HAP ≥48 hours hospitalized; VAP ≥48 hours after intubation
Prior MRSA/Pseudomonas isolation or recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics → resistant pathogens

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, cough, sputum, focal crackles; older adults: confusion; children: lower-lobe disease may refer abdominal pain
★ Severe: **hypoxemia, hypotension, tachypnea**, multilobar disease; ventilation or pressors → ICU
Legionella: water exposure, diarrhea, hyponatremia; Mycoplasma: school-age/young adult, indolent dry cough, cold agglutinins
Immunocompromised, diffuse bilateral interstitial/alveolar infiltrates, exertional hypoxemia → **Pneumocystis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alveolar inflammation/exudate → shunt and impaired oxygenation
Chemical aspiration pneumonitis: sterile gastric injury; severity tracks **volume and acidity**; rapid improvement possible

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CXR** first; CT if strong suspicion despite nondiagnostic radiograph
**CURB-65** 0–1 or low PSI → outpatient; severe CAP → blood/sputum cultures, Legionella antigen ± PCR
Low procalcitonin alone does not justify withholding initial antibiotics in radiographically confirmed bacterial CAP
Gram-positive lancet diplococci → **S pneumoniae**: commonest CAP; lobar consolidation, high fever, often post-viral URI
Small gram-negative coccobacilli, smoker/COPD → **H influenzae**

rows.label: Tx
items: Oxygen, fluids for hypoperfusion; drain empyema; narrow antibiotics to cultures
★ Aspiration pneumonia: usual CAP coverage; **add anaerobic coverage only for abscess/empyema**
Anaerobes: **ampicillin-sulbactam**; older exam questions may expect **clindamycin**, even without abscess
Stable nonsevere CAP: ATS 2025 permits 3–4 days; classic ≥5-day rule remains for severe disease
★ Severe noninfluenza CAP → consider **systemic corticosteroids**; nonsevere CAP → avoid routine steroids

rows.label: Complications
items: Parapneumonic effusion, empyema, bacteremia, respiratory failure, sepsis
S aureus: postinfluenza necrotizing pneumonia; child failing amoxicillin, dense consolidation/effusion
Aspiration (alcoholism, intubation) → **lung abscess**: dependent-segment cavity, air-fluid level, foul sputum
Antibiotic exposure → C difficile

rows.label: Prevention
items: Influenza/pneumococcal vaccination, smoking cessation, swallowing evaluation
Aspiration/VAP prevention: head elevation 30–45°, oral care, early liberation from ventilation

rows.label: Mimics
items: PE: thrombotic risk, pleuritic pain, no infectious source
HF: bilateral edema, elevated JVP, cardiac dysfunction

table.title: Empiric adult regimens
rows: Amoxicillin/clavulanate + azithromycin; doxycycline alternative; or levofloxacin
Antipseudomonal: cefepime, ceftazidime, or piperacillin/tazobactam; usually 7 days

polycystic-kidney-disease.name: Polycystic kidney disease
polycystic-kidney-disease.scope: Autosomal dominant PKD, 50% inheritance risk, hypertension control, berry aneurysms, hepatic cysts, MVP, tolvaptan
polycystic-kidney-disease.core: Autosomal dominant cystic kidney disease produces progressive bilateral renal enlargement and systemic manifestations; family history guides diagnosis and targeted screening.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heterozygous PKD1 or PKD2 variants; each child has 50% transmission risk
PKD1 generally progresses earlier; hypertension, large kidney volume and early renal decline predict worse course

rows.label: Clues
items: Flank discomfort, palpable kidneys, recurrent hematuria, stones, UTIs or early hypertension
★ Fever and persistent focal pain → **cyst infection**, even with nondiagnostic urine culture
Sudden severe headache/meningeal signs → possible aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage; emergency evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormal polycystin signaling promotes tubular cyst expansion and interstitial fibrosis
Intrarenal ischemia activates RAAS; cyst burden progressively reduces functional nephron mass

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Renal ultrasound** first with family history; MRI/CT if equivocal or for kidney-volume assessment
Monitor BP, creatinine/eGFR, urine albumin; genetic testing when uncertain diagnosis or reproductive/donor decisions
★ Aneurysm screening with **noncontrast MRA** for personal SAH or family aneurysm/SAH/unexplained sudden death
Do not routinely screen every patient for intracranial aneurysm; discuss additional individualized risk contexts

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **ACE inhibitor or ARB** for hypertension, especially albuminuria; avoid during pregnancy
Rapidly progressive adult disease with eGFR ≥25 → consider **tolvaptan**; monitor liver tests, polyuria and dehydration
Cyst infection → cyst-penetrating antibiotic such as ciprofloxacin based on cultures; drain refractory large infected cyst
Hematuria → rest, hydration and exclude stone/tumor if persistent; severe bleeding → embolization
Advanced kidney failure → dialysis/transplant evaluation; avoid chronic NSAIDs

rows.label: Complications
items: **CKD → ESKD** most common long-term complication; hepatic cysts, intracranial aneurysms, MVP, diverticulosis, infection
Tolvaptan → hepatotoxicity and aquaresis; aneurysm rupture → catastrophic hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Genetic/reproductive counseling; smoking cessation, sodium reduction, BP control; avoid dehydration on aquaretic treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Simple cysts: few incidental lesions without enlarged kidneys/familial pattern
ARPKD: neonate, bilateral enlarged echogenic kidneys, congenital hepatic fibrosis
Acquired cystic disease: longstanding CKD/dialysis
Wilms tumor/neuroblastoma: solid, usually unilateral mass, not bilateral cystic nephromegaly

primary-immunodeficiencies.name: Primary immunodeficiencies
primary-immunodeficiencies.scope: Selective IgA deficiency, common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), X-linked agammaglobulinemia, severe combined immunodeficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich, chronic granulomatous disease
primary-immunodeficiencies.core: Recurrent, unusually severe, persistent, or opportunistic infections; organism pattern and age of onset localize the immune defect.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Consanguinity, affected relatives, male relatives dying in infancy; absent family history does not exclude disease

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, persistent thrush, or infections across multiple organ systems
Deep abscesses suggest phagocyte dysfunction; recurrent encapsulated bacteria suggest impaired antibody function

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Selective IgA deficiency: impaired mucosal defense; respiratory infections, giardiasis, atopy, or no symptoms
Antibody disorders impair opsonization; T-cell defects permit viral, fungal, and protozoal opportunists
DiGeorge: 3rd/4th **pharyngeal pouch** failure → absent thymus, hypocalcemia, conotruncal defects, T-cell infections
ADA deficiency: autosomal recessive SCID; toxic deoxyadenosine destroys T and B cells

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Start **CBC with differential, quantitative immunoglobulins**, HIV testing; assess vaccine antibody responses
Lymphocyte subsets distinguish B-cell and T-cell deficiencies; abnormal results → genetic confirmation
IgA deficiency: isolated IgA <7 mg/dL after age 4 years; normal IgG and IgM
★ Newborn **TREC screen** detects impaired T-cell production before symptomatic SCID

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Profound combined immune failure → isolation, irradiated CMV-negative blood products, urgent **transplant evaluation**
Acute infections: organism-directed antimicrobials; immunoglobulin replacement not useful for isolated IgA deficiency

rows.label: Complications
items: Bronchiectasis, chronic enteropathy, autoimmune disease; CVID additionally increases lymphoma risk
Anti-IgA antibodies can cause anaphylaxis to blood products

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Avoid **live vaccines** in major T-cell defects; immunize household contacts with safe vaccine choices
IgA-related transfusion reactions → washed cellular products or IgA-deficient plasma
CGD: TMP-SMX + itraconazole prophylaxis; genetic counseling for inherited defects

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vertical HIV: bacterial infections + zoster, nodes, maternal opportunistic infection; low CD4, positive virologic testing
Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia: nephrotic protein loss, B-cell malignancy, or rituximab exposure

table.title: Defect fingerprints
rows: Adolescent/adult; low IgG, poor vaccine response
Boy after 6 months; absent tonsils/B cells
Infant; absent thymic shadow, profound lymphopenia
Cold abscesses, eczema, retained teeth, pneumatoceles

primary-immunodeficiencies.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical immunology teaching.

rickets.name: Rickets
rickets.scope: Nutritional vitamin D deficiency, X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets, metaphyseal cupping and fraying, elevated alkaline phosphatase, low phosphate, high PTH
rickets.core: Growing child with bowed legs, widened wrists, and delayed growth: evaluate defective growth-plate mineralization rather than treating the deformity alone.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ Nutritional: **unsupplemented breastfeeding**, low dietary calcium, limited sunlight, darker skin, malabsorption
Inherited phosphate wasting: X-linked dominant; affected fathers transmit to all daughters, no sons

rows.label: Clues
items: Rachitic rosary, craniotabes, delayed fontanelle closure, bone pain, hypotonia, delayed walking
Hypocalcemic tetany, seizures, prolonged QT, cardiomyopathy → urgent stabilization
Persistent short stature, lower-limb deformity, dental abscesses despite adequate vitamin D → phosphate-wasting disorder

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nutritional deficiency → reduced intestinal calcium absorption → secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal phosphate loss
**PHEX mutation → excess FGF23**, renal phosphaturia and inappropriately low calcitriol

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Wrist/knee radiograph → **metaphyseal cupping, fraying, widened growth plates**
★ Check **calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, 25-OH vitamin D**, creatinine; ALP elevated, phosphate reduced
25-OH vitamin D <12 ng/mL supports deficiency; interpret with calcium intake and biochemical pattern
Normal vitamin D with hypophosphatemia → assess renal phosphate wasting; genetic evaluation if inherited pattern

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic hypocalcemia → **IV calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring**, then oral calcium
During repletion → repeat calcium/phosphate/ALP; assess radiographic healing
Burosumab must not accompany oral phosphate/active vitamin D; specialist monitoring prevents excess phosphate
Persistent renal disease/acidosis → treat cause; orthopedic correction only for residual deformity after metabolic control

rows.label: Complications
items: Fractures, permanent deformity, impaired growth; severe hypocalcemia → arrhythmia
Phosphate/calcitriol: ↑PTH, hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis → urine calcium and renal ultrasound monitoring

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Infants: **vitamin D 400 IU/day**; after 12 months, total intake 600 IU/day plus calcium-rich foods
Maternal nutrition, supplementation during malabsorption, and family counseling for inherited disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: Physiologic bowing: symmetric toddler legs, normal growth plates/laboratory studies
Blount disease: focal medial tibial growth disturbance, often obesity; normal mineral studies
Osteogenesis imperfecta: fragile collagen, blue sclerae; no characteristic growth-plate changes

septic-arthritis.name: Septic arthritis
septic-arthritis.scope: Nongonococcal, gonococcal, prosthetic joint infection, IV drug use, empiric coverage (vancomycin + cefepime), contiguous osteomyelitis
septic-arthritis.core: Acutely painful swollen joint with restricted passive motion → urgent aspiration and drainage; delayed treatment rapidly destroys cartilage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prosthesis, recent surgery/injection, rheumatoid arthritis, immunosuppression, diabetes, bacteremia
IV drug use → S aureus and gram-negative risk, including Pseudomonas
Young sexually active adults → disseminated gonorrhea; adjacent ulcers/osteomyelitis → contiguous spread
RA joint with new febrile monoarthritis → infection until aspirated, not flare

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually acute monoarthritis, often knee; fever may be absent, especially in older/immunocompromised adults
★ **Severe pain with both active and passive motion**; inability to bear weight; child's hip held flexed, abducted, externally rotated
Gonococcal dissemination: migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, sparse pustules; may progress to purulent monoarthritis
Prosthetic infection: persistent pain, loosening, wound drainage or sinus tract, sometimes minimal systemic illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hematogenous seeding or direct inoculation → neutrophilic enzymes damage articular cartilage
Implant biofilm limits antibiotic eradication without surgical source control
★ **S aureus** most common, including RA-damaged joints: gram-positive cocci in clusters
Asplenia or recent pharyngitis → **streptococci**: gram-positive cocci in chains

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Arthrocentesis before antibiotics** when stable: cell count/differential, Gram stain, culture, crystals
Synovial WBC >50,000/µL, neutrophil predominance supports infection; lower counts or negative Gram stain never exclude
★ **Crystals do not exclude infection**; send cultures even when gout seems likely
Blood cultures; gonococcal: aspirate on **chocolate/Thayer-Martin agar** plus mucosal NAAT; MRI for suspected contiguous osteomyelitis
New warmth/effusion in OA joint → aspirate before any intra-articular steroid

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ After cultures → **IV vancomycin + cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam** for severe disease, IV drug use, gram-negative risk
Stable low-risk adult: vancomycin ± ceftriaxone based on exposure; narrow to organism/susceptibility
Sepsis → immediate antibiotics without delaying for aspiration; large joints: arthroscopic washout; **hip → operative drainage**, not serial aspiration
Persistent symptoms → repeat drainage, seek abscess/osteomyelitis; mobilize after infection controlled

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible joint destruction, avascular necrosis, osteomyelitis, bacteremia, sepsis
Prolonged antibiotics → renal injury, line complications, C difficile; prolonged immobility → stiffness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sterile procedures, treat skin infections, injection-harm reduction
Gonorrhea: treat partners, screen other STIs, abstain until treatment completed and partners treated

rows.label: Mimics
items: Crystal arthritis: polarized crystals; infection still possible concurrently
Bursitis: localized periarticular swelling, passive joint motion relatively preserved
Reactive arthritis: sterile inflammatory arthritis after GI/GU infection
Transient synovitis (child): afebrile, bears weight, ESR <40, WBC <12,000

table.title: Special treatment branches
rows: Debridement, implant retention, prolonged pathogen-directed antibiotics

stevens-johnson-syndrome.name: Stevens-Johnson syndrome
stevens-johnson-syndrome.scope: SJS and TEN (<10% vs >30% BSA detachment), culprit drugs (antibiotics, anticonvulsants, allopurinol), mucosal involvement, Nikolsky sign, burn unit management
stevens-johnson-syndrome.core: Recent medication exposure, fever, and rapidly spreading tender dusky macules; epidermal necrolysis severity follows detached surface area.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually 1–4 weeks after starting sulfonamides/antibiotics, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, phenytoin, allopurinol, NSAIDs
Previous reaction, HIV; risk modified by drug-specific HLA susceptibility

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Painful erosions, ≥2 mucosal sites (oral, ocular, genital)**; flat atypical targets, flaccid bullae, sheet-like sloughing
★ **Nikolsky sign**: epidermis shears with gentle lateral pressure; not specific to SJS/TEN
Dysphonia, secretion intolerance, hypoxemia → airway involvement; tachycardia/hypotension → systemic deterioration

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Drug-triggered cytotoxic T cells/NK cells release granulysin and related mediators → widespread keratinocyte apoptosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical emergency; **skin biopsy** confirms full-thickness epidermal necrosis and subepidermal separation
Count detached/detachable skin, not total erythematous area; document every mucosal site
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, bicarbonate, glucose, LFTs; cultures for suspected infection; SCORTEN estimates mortality

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Stop culprit/nonessential drugs immediately**; urgent dermatology, burn/ICU assessment; extensive loss → specialized unit
Airway assessment, IV crystalloid titrated to perfusion, electrolyte replacement, warming, analgesia, early enteral nutrition
Nonadherent wound care, minimize skin trauma; **urgent ophthalmology** for lubrication and ocular-surface protection
Systemic antibiotics only for clinical infection; no routine prophylaxis or routine thermal-burn fluid formulas
Cyclosporine/etanercept or other immunomodulation: specialist decision; no universal regimen; never delay supportive care

rows.label: Complications
items: Sepsis, fluid/electrolyte losses, AKI, respiratory failure, death; risk increases with greater epidermal loss
Corneal scarring/blindness, symblepharon, genital/urinary strictures, pigment/nail changes, psychological sequelae

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Document **permanent culprit avoidance**, related-drug review, medical alert identification; never diagnostic rechallenge
Carbamazepine, at-risk Asian ancestry → HLA-B*15:02 screening; positive → choose alternative
Allopurinol: HLA-B*58:01 screening for African American, Han Chinese, Korean, Thai ancestry

rows.label: Mimics
items: Staphylococcal scalded skin: infants, superficial cleavage, mucosa spared
Erythema multiforme: raised classic targets, acral distribution, often HSV-triggered
DRESS: eosinophilia, facial edema, hepatitis; usually no extensive epidermal detachment
Kawasaki disease: ≥5 days fever, nonexudative conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue; no mucosal erosions or culprit drug

supraventricular-tachycardia.name: Supraventricular tachycardia
supraventricular-tachycardia.scope: AVNRT, AVRT, focal atrial tachycardia, vagal maneuvers, adenosine, synchronized cardioversion, catheter ablation
supraventricular-tachycardia.core: Abrupt rapid regular palpitations with a usually narrow QRS often represent AV-node-dependent reentry; stability determines immediate electrical versus pharmacologic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Accessory pathway, prior episodes, adrenergic triggers, caffeine/stimulants
Focal atrial tachycardia may accompany structural disease; incessant forms can cause cardiomyopathy

rows.label: Clues
items: Regular rate often 150–250/min; palpitations, lightheadedness, dyspnea, neck pounding
★ **Hypotension, shock, ischemic chest pain, altered mentation**, or acute HF → unstable tachycardia
WPW between episodes: short PR, delta wave, widened QRS; may be absent with concealed pathway

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reentry requires distinct conduction/refractory properties; AV node participates in AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT
Adenosine transiently blocks AV conduction; automatic atrial rhythms may continue despite transient ventricular slowing

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **12-lead ECG during episode**, continuous rhythm monitoring; check electrolytes, medication/exposure triggers
Wide-complex rhythm uncertain → presume VT rather than casually applying narrow-complex algorithm
Structural concern → echocardiography; recurrent undocumented events → ambulatory monitoring/electrophysiology evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable with pulse → **synchronized cardioversion**; sedation if feasible without delaying rescue
★ Stable regular narrow rhythm → **modified Valsalva → rapid IV adenosine**
Persistent stable SVT → IV diltiazem/verapamil or beta blocker if no contraindication; cardioversion if unsuccessful
★ Irregular wide preexcited AF → **procainamide or cardioversion**; avoid AV-nodal blockers, including adenosine
Recurrent symptomatic AVNRT/AVRT or focal tachycardia → catheter ablation; selected patients use oral nodal blockers

rows.label: Complications
items: Syncope, demand ischemia, tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy; preexcited AF can degenerate to VF
Adenosine: brief flushing/chest pressure, bronchospasm; avoid in active severe bronchospasm

rows.label: Prevention
items: Teach vagal maneuver, limit personal triggers; discuss definitive ablation for recurrence
Ablation near AV node carries small heart-block risk; shared procedural decision

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sinus tachycardia: gradual rate changes, beat-to-beat variability, physiologic driver; infants rarely >220/min
Atrial flutter: atrial sawtooth waves, often ventricular rate near 150

supraventricular-tachycardia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AHA adult advanced life support](https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support), [ACC/AHA AF guideline (2023)](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2023.08.017).

testicular-cancer.name: Testicular cancer
testicular-cancer.scope: Seminoma, nonseminomatous germ cell tumors, sex cord-stromal tumors (Leydig cell, Sertoli cell), tumor markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH), scrotal ultrasound, radical inguinal orchiectomy
testicular-cancer.core: A solid intratesticular lesion requires urgent evaluation for malignancy; an inguinal approach preserves proper staging and lymphatic drainage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Cryptorchidism**, prior contralateral germ cell tumor, family history, testicular dysgenesis
Most germ cell tumors arise in young adults; older men also require consideration of lymphoma

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually painless firm enlargement or heaviness; pain does not exclude malignancy
Gynecomastia from hormone production; back pain may indicate retroperitoneal nodes
Cough/dyspnea, supraclavicular nodes suggest dissemination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Most adult tumors germ cell-derived; mixed tumors managed as nonseminomatous
Lymphatic spread follows gonadal vessels to retroperitoneal para-aortic nodes rather than initial inguinal drainage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler** first distinguishes intratesticular from extratesticular lesions
★ **AFP, β-hCG, LDH before orchiectomy**; repeat afterward for staging and response
CT abdomen/pelvis + chest imaging for metastases; normal markers do not exclude cancer
Avoid transscrotal needle biopsy or scrotal orchiectomy; disrupted lymphatics complicate treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Radical inguinal orchiectomy** for suspicious solid mass; discuss sperm banking before gonadotoxic treatment
Stage I seminoma: surveillance preferred when reliable; carboplatin or radiation selected alternatives
Stage I nonseminoma: surveillance, cisplatin-based chemotherapy, or retroperitoneal node dissection according to risk
★ Metastatic germ cell tumor → cisplatin-based **BEP**; residual nonseminomatous mass may require resection
Sex cord-stromal tumors: surgery; monitor endocrine manifestations and malignant features

rows.label: Complications
items: Infertility, hypogonadism; assess contralateral function
BEP: bleomycin pulmonary toxicity; cisplatin nephrotoxicity/ototoxicity; etoposide-associated leukemia
Retroperitoneal node surgery may cause retrograde ejaculation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Orchiopexy reduces cryptorchid-associated risk but does not eliminate it; no routine population screening
Strict stage-specific surveillance with examination, markers, and imaging after treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hydrocele: transilluminates; ultrasound needed if testis not palpable
Epididymitis: tender epididymis, urinary/infectious symptoms
Torsion: abrupt severe pain, absent cremasteric reflex; immediate exploration when strongly suspected

thrombocytopenia.name: Thrombocytopenia
thrombocytopenia.scope: Evaluation of isolated thrombocytopenia, peripheral smear, immune thrombocytopenia, drug-induced, procedural platelet thresholds
thrombocytopenia.core: Low platelet count requires confirmation and distinction among impaired production, immune destruction, consumption, sequestration, and laboratory artifact.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent infection, autoimmune disease, HIV/HCV, lymphoproliferative disease → secondary immune thrombocytopenia
Heparin, quinine, TMP-SMX, vancomycin; alcohol, marrow-suppressive drugs; cirrhosis with splenic sequestration

rows.label: Clues
items: Petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gingival bleeding; mucosal hemorrhage signals clinically important platelet disorder
★ **Neurologic/renal abnormalities + hemolysis** → thrombotic microangiopathy; systemic illness/coagulopathy → DIC
Heparin exposure + >50% platelet decline, thrombosis, typical 5–10-day onset → HIT

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ITP: IgG platelet clearance, impaired megakaryocytes; maternal IgG crosses placenta → **fetal platelet destruction**
Drug-dependent immune destruction often causes abrupt severe counts; HIT: anti-PF4/heparin IgG activates platelets, producing thrombosis
**Kasabach-Merritt**: infant vascular tumor (kaposiform hemangioendothelioma/tufted angioma; older exams: hemangioma) traps platelets → severe thrombocytopenia, consumptive coagulopathy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Repeat CBC + peripheral smear**; platelet clumps → citrate tube for pseudothrombocytopenia
Isolated low platelets, normal coagulation, large platelets → ITP after excluding secondary causes
Schistocytes → LDH, haptoglobin, creatinine, coagulation studies; suspected TTP → urgent ADAMTS13 sample
HIV/HCV testing for new ITP; marrow biopsy only atypical cytopenias or suspected marrow disease
4Ts estimates HIT probability; intermediate/high → PF4 immunoassay, functional confirmation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adult ITP **<30,000/µL or bleeding → glucocorticoid**; children without significant bleeding → observation
★ ITP critical bleeding → **IVIG + high-dose steroid + platelet transfusion**
Drug immune thrombocytopenia → stop culprit; persistent ITP → rituximab, thrombopoietin agonist, or selected splenectomy
Suspected TTP → plasma exchange; HIT → stop heparin, start argatroban/nonheparin anticoagulant
Older board LP target: 50,000/µL; current trigger below; neurosurgical targets often ≥100,000/µL

rows.label: Complications
items: Intracranial hemorrhage with severe disease; thrombosis in HIT/TTP
Steroid toxicity, immunosuppression; splenectomy → encapsulated bacterial sepsis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid culprit rechallenge, aspirin/NSAIDs when bleeding risk high; vaccinate before splenectomy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Von Willebrand disease: often normal platelet count with mucocutaneous bleeding
Marrow failure: additional cytopenias, abnormal precursor morphology

thrombocytopenia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AABB/ICTMG platelet recommendations (2025)](https://www.aabb.org/news-resources/news/article/2025/05/29/aabb-develops-new-platelet-transfusion-guidelines); other hematology principles not separately checked.

thrombotic-microangiopathies.name: Thrombotic microangiopathies
thrombotic-microangiopathies.scope: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (ADAMTS13, pentad, plasma exchange), hemolytic uremic syndrome (shiga toxin, supportive care), atypical HUS, schistocytes, MAHA
thrombotic-microangiopathies.core: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia plus thrombocytopenia and organ injury: urgently distinguish TTP, Shiga toxin-associated HUS, and complement-mediated HUS.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Immune TTP: acquired ADAMTS13 autoantibody; autoimmune disease, pregnancy, HIV can trigger episodes
STEC-HUS: contaminated food/water, often children; recurrent episodes suggest inherited complement susceptibility
Secondary TMA: severe hypertension, pregnancy complications, transplant, calcineurin inhibitors or other drugs

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Schistocytes**, ↑LDH/indirect bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin, reticulocytosis; direct antiglobulin test usually negative
TTP often neurologic/cardiac-predominant; HUS often renal-predominant, with substantial overlap
Classical TTP pentad: hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, fever, neurologic changes, renal dysfunction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Platelet-rich microthrombi shear passing erythrocytes and obstruct small-vessel perfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: CBC/smear, hemolysis studies, creatinine, urinalysis, PT/aPTT/fibrinogen; coagulation usually normal unlike DIC
★ **High PLASMIC score** supports empiric TTP management while awaiting definitive testing
ECG/troponin and neurologic examination assess otherwise occult organ injury
Normal complement levels do not exclude atypical HUS

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected immune TTP → **treat immediately**; do not await full pentad or confirmatory result
★ STEC disease: **avoid antibiotics/antimotility drugs**; RBC transfusion for symptomatic anemia
TTP: no platelets unless life-threatening bleeding; plasma infusion only if exchange unavoidably delayed

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, myocardial ischemia, seizures, renal failure, death; survivors may develop CKD or cognitive impairment
Caplacizumab → bleeding; complement inhibition → meningococcal infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: TTP remission → monitor ADAMTS13/relapse symptoms; treat marked recurrent deficiency with hematology
★ Before complement blockade: **MenACWY + MenB**; urgent start before vaccine protection → penicillin prophylaxis
Food safety and hand hygiene reduce STEC exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: DIC: prolonged clotting times, low fibrinogen, systemic coagulation activation
HELLP: pregnancy-associated hypertension, elevated liver enzymes; delivery central to treatment
B12 deficiency: macrocytosis, low reticulocyte response despite striking LDH

table.title: Decisive subtype branches
rows: Urgent plasma exchange + steroids, caplacizumab, rituximab
Shiga injury; often after bloody diarrhea
